**Surah al-Tur** is Meccan, and it has forty-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By Mount Sinai (al-Tur)﴾ ﴿and by a Book inscribed﴾ ﴿on parchment unrolled﴾ ﴿and by the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur)﴾ ﴿and by the raised canopy﴾ ﴿and by the sea set aflame﴾ ﴿indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall﴾ ﴿none can avert it﴾ ﴿on the day the sky will sway violently﴾ ﴿and the mountains will move away, moving﴾ ﴿woe on that day to the deniers﴾ ﴿who are playing around in their vain talk﴾ ﴿the day they will be pushed headlong into the fire of Hell﴾ ﴿"This is the Fire which you used to deny!"﴾ ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ ﴿Burn in it, and be patient or be impatient; it is the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and bliss﴾ ﴿enjoying what their Lord has given them, and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction, for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows, and We will marry them to fair maidens with wide, lovely eyes.﴾ ﴿And those who believed, and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join their offspring with them, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned.﴾ ﴿And We will provide them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿They will pass around among themselves a cup, in which there is no idle talk and no sin.﴾ [Al-Tur: 23] ﴿And there will go around among them young boys (ghilman) belonging to them, as if they were pearls well-guarded.﴾ [Al-Tur: 24] ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other.﴾ [Al-Tur: 25] ﴿They will say, "Indeed, we were, before, fearful among our families.﴾ [Al-Tur: 26] ﴿So Allah bestowed favor upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾ [Al-Tur: 27] ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful."﴾ [Al-Tur: 28]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is clear, since at the end of the previous surah (al-Dhariyat) Allah says: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion like the portion of their companions﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 59], and here He says: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall.﴾

*Al-Tur* means the mountain. The apparent meaning is that it is a generic noun (ism jins), not a specific mountain, although in Syria there is a mountain called al-Tur, namely Tur Sinai. Nawf al-Bikali said: it is the one by which Allah swore, because of its superiority over the other mountains. It is said that it is the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa (peace be upon him).

*Al-Kitab al-Mastur* (the inscribed Book) may refer to the Qur'an, or to what has been copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or to the Torah, or it is the Gospel and the Psalms, or it is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded, or the scrolls given on the Day of Resurrection in the right hand and the left. The last of these opinions is that of al-Farra'. None of these should be specified definitively; they are presented only as possibilities.

Abu al-Sammal recited *fi riqqin* with a kasra on the *ra'*. *Manshur* means spread out. It is also said: open, with no seal on it. It is also said: manifest, clear. From Ibn 'Abbas: "unrolled, extending between the East and the West."

As for *al-Bayt al-Ma'mur* (the frequented House), 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: it is a house in the heavens, directly above the Ka'bah, called *al-Durah*, and also *al-Darih*, and this is the one mentioned in the hadith of the Isra' (Night Journey). Jibril said: "This is the frequented House; seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and then they never return to it again, until the last of them." Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: in every heaven there is a frequented House, and in every earth there is likewise. Ibn al-Kawwa asked 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "It is a house above the seven heavens, beneath the Throne, called al-Darih." Al-Hasan said: the frequented House is the Ka'bah, which Allah causes to be visited every year by six hundred thousand, and if people fail to do so, Allah completes it with angels.

*Al-Saqf al-Marfu'* (the raised canopy): it is the heaven. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Throne, and it is the ceiling of Paradise.

*Al-Bahr al-Masjur* (the sea set aflame): Mujahid, Shimr ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Akhfash said: it is the sea kindled with fire. It is also narrated that the sea is Hell. Qatadah said: *al-masjur* means "filled." This is well known in the language, and al-Tabari preferred it, on the basis that the water of the sea is indeed like that. It does not contradict what Mujahid said, because *sajarta al-tannur* means: you filled the oven with what burns. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masjur* is that whose water has gone away. Dhu al-Rummah the poet narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A slave-woman went out to draw water, and she said: 'The pool is *masjur*,' meaning empty." Dhu al-Rummah has no narration except this one, so it is one of the words with contrary meanings (al-adda'). It is narrated that the seas' water will go away on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas also said: *al-masjur* is the restrained, from which comes *sajur al-kalb*, the dog's collar of wood or iron that holds it back; and were it not that the sea is held back, it would overflow onto the earth. Al-Rabi' said: *al-masjur* is the mixture of sweet water with salt water. It is also said: *al-mafjur* (the burst), and this is supported by: ﴿And when the seas are burst open﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. The majority hold that the sea sworn by is the sea of this world, and this is supported by: ﴿And when the seas are set aflame﴾ [al-Takwir: 6]. From 'Ali and Ibn 'Umar: it is in the heaven beneath the Throne, containing a thick water called the Sea of Life, from which the servants will be rained upon for forty mornings after the first blast, and they will sprout up in their graves. Qutaybah ibn Sa'id said: it is Hell, and it was called a sea because of its vastness and its waves, as is said of the horse: "And if we find it truly a sea." It is said that the sentence may be in the oaths by the Tur, the sea and the House, because these are places of solitude with Allah, from which their Lord spoke to His messengers.

So at Mount Tur, Musa said: ﴿Show me, let me look upon You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]; the frequented House belongs to Muhammad (ﷺ); and the sea set aflame belongs to Yunus, who said: ﴿There is no deity but You; glory be to You﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. These places were honored for these reasons. The oath by the inscribed Book is because the prophets (peace be upon them) had speech with Allah in these places, and its being coupled with the Tur indicates this. The oath by the raised canopy is to show the elevation of the frequented House. End.

He made *wa-kitabin* indefinite, because it encompasses every Book that Allah sent down, by way of substitution (shumul al-badal). It may also be a comprehensive inclusion (shumul al-'umum), like His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

Its being *fi riqq* indicates its permanence, and that it does not go beyond heads. Describing it as *manshur* indicates its clarity, unlike a folded book whose contents are unknown; an unrolled book has its contents known, and nothing prevents reading what it contains. The first *waw* is the *waw* of oath, and what follows it is for coordination (al-'atf). The sentence sworn to is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall.﴾

There is a subtle point in the attachment of the punishment to *Rabbika* (your Lord), since He is the Owner and the One who oversees the servant's welfare. By the attachment to the Lord, and its attachment to the pronoun of address (kaf al-khitab), there is reassurance for him (ﷺ). Indeed the punishment is certain to befall those who denied him, and it is *waqi'* (befalling) with severity; this word is more indicative of that than *la-ka'in* (certainly existing). Do you not see His saying: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1], and His saying: ﴿And it will befall them﴾ [al-Shura: 22]? It is as if it is prepared in an elevated place, and it falls upon whoever it lands on.

From Jubayr ibn Mut'im: "I came to Madinah to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the prisoners of Badr. I found him reciting in the Maghrib prayer: ﴿By the Tur﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall, none can avert it﴾, and it was as if my heart was split open. So I embraced Islam out of fear of the descent of the punishment, and I did not think I would rise from my place before the punishment would befall me." Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *waqi'un* without the lam. Qatadah said: he means the punishment of the Hereafter for the disbelievers, i.e., it is certain to befall upon the disbelievers.

Dhu al-Rummah the poet narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A slave-woman went out to draw water, and she said: 'The pool is *masjur*,' meaning empty." Dhu al-Rummah has no narration except this one, so it is one of the words with contrary meanings (al-adda'). It is narrated that the seas' water will go away on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas also said: *al-masjur* is the restrained, from which comes *sajur al-kalb*, the dog's collar of wood or iron that holds it back; and were it not that the sea is held back, it would overflow onto the earth. Al-Rabi' said: *al-masjur* is the mixture of sweet water with salt water. It is also said: *al-mafjur* (the burst), and this is supported by: ﴿And when the seas are burst open﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. The majority hold that the sea sworn by is the sea of this world, and this is supported by: ﴿And when the seas are set aflame﴾ [al-Takwir: 6]. From 'Ali and Ibn 'Umar: it is in the heaven beneath the Throne, containing a thick water called the Sea of Life, from which the servants will be rained upon for forty mornings after the first blast, and they will sprout up in their graves. Qutaybah ibn Sa'id said: it is Hell, and it was called a sea because of its vastness and its waves, as is said of the horse: "And if we find it truly a sea." It is said that the sentence may be in the oaths by the Tur, the sea and the House, because these are places of solitude with Allah, from which their Lord spoke to His messengers.

So at Mount Tur, Musa said: ﴿Show me, let me look upon You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]; the frequented House belongs to Muhammad (ﷺ); and the sea set aflame belongs to Yunus, who said: ﴿There is no deity but You; glory be to You﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. These places were honored for these reasons. The oath by the inscribed Book is because the prophets (peace be upon them) had speech with Allah in these places, and its being coupled with the Tur indicates this. The oath by the raised canopy is to show the elevation of the frequented House. End.

He made *wa-kitabin* indefinite, because it encompasses every Book that Allah sent down, by way of substitution (shumul al-badal). It may also be a comprehensive inclusion (shumul al-'umum), like His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

Its being *fi riqq* indicates its permanence, and that it does not go beyond heads. Describing it as *manshur* indicates its clarity, unlike a folded book whose contents are unknown; an unrolled book has its contents known, and nothing prevents reading what it contains. The first *waw* is the *waw* of oath, and what follows it is for coordination (al-'atf). The sentence sworn to is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall.﴾

There is a subtle point in the attachment of the punishment to *Rabbika* (your Lord), since He is the Owner and the One who oversees the servant's welfare. By the attachment to the Lord, and its attachment to the pronoun of address (kaf al-khitab), there is reassurance for him (ﷺ). Indeed the punishment is certain to befall those who denied him, and it is *waqi'* (befalling) with severity; this word is more indicative of that than *la-ka'in* (certainly existing). Do you not see His saying: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1], and His saying: ﴿And it will befall them﴾ [al-Shura: 22]? It is as if it is prepared in an elevated place, and it falls upon whoever it lands on.

From Jubayr ibn Mut'im: "I came to Madinah to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the prisoners of Badr. I found him reciting in the Maghrib prayer: ﴿By the Tur﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall, none can avert it﴾, and it was as if my heart was split open. So I embraced Islam out of fear of the descent of the punishment, and I did not think I would rise from my place before the punishment would befall me." Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *waqi'un* without the lam. Qatadah said: he means the punishment of the Hereafter for the disbelievers, i.e., it is certain to befall upon the disbelievers.

**Surah al-Tur** is Meccan, and it has forty-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By Mount Sinai (al-Tur)﴾ ﴿and by a Book inscribed﴾ ﴿on parchment unrolled﴾ ﴿and by the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur)﴾ ﴿and by the raised canopy﴾ ﴿and by the sea set aflame﴾ ﴿indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall﴾ ﴿none can avert it﴾ ﴿on the day the sky will sway violently﴾ ﴿and the mountains will move away, moving﴾ ﴿woe on that day to the deniers﴾ ﴿who are playing around in their vain talk﴾ ﴿the day they will be pushed headlong into the fire of Hell﴾ ﴿"This is the Fire which you used to deny!"﴾ ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ ﴿Burn in it, and be patient or be impatient; it is the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and bliss﴾ ﴿enjoying what their Lord has given them, and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction, for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows, and We will marry them to fair maidens with wide, lovely eyes.﴾ ﴿And those who believed, and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join their offspring with them, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned.﴾ ﴿And We will provide them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿They will pass around among themselves a cup, in which there is no idle talk and no sin.﴾ [Al-Tur: 23] ﴿And there will go around among them young boys (ghilman) belonging to them, as if they were pearls well-guarded.﴾ [Al-Tur: 24] ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other.﴾ [Al-Tur: 25] ﴿They will say, "Indeed, we were, before, fearful among our families.﴾ [Al-Tur: 26] ﴿So Allah bestowed favor upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾ [Al-Tur: 27] ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful."﴾ [Al-Tur: 28]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is clear, since at the end of the previous surah (al-Dhariyat) Allah says: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion like the portion of their companions﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 59], and here He says: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall.﴾

*Al-Tur* means the mountain. The apparent meaning is that it is a generic noun (ism jins), not a specific mountain, although in Syria there is a mountain called al-Tur, namely Tur Sinai. Nawf al-Bikali said: it is the one by which Allah swore, because of its superiority over the other mountains. It is said that it is the mountain on which Allah spoke to Musa (peace be upon him).

*Al-Kitab al-Mastur* (the inscribed Book) may refer to the Qur'an, or to what has been copied from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or to the Torah, or it is the Gospel and the Psalms, or it is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded, or the scrolls given on the Day of Resurrection in the right hand and the left. The last of these opinions is that of al-Farra'. None of these should be specified definitively; they are presented only as possibilities.

Abu al-Sammal recited *fi riqqin* with a kasra on the *ra'*. *Manshur* means spread out. It is also said: open, with no seal on it. It is also said: manifest, clear. From Ibn 'Abbas: "unrolled, extending between the East and the West."

As for *al-Bayt al-Ma'mur* (the frequented House), 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: it is a house in the heavens, directly above the Ka'bah, called *al-Durah*, and also *al-Darih*, and this is the one mentioned in the hadith of the Isra' (Night Journey). Jibril said: "This is the frequented House; seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and then they never return to it again, until the last of them." Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: in every heaven there is a frequented House, and in every earth there is likewise. Ibn al-Kawwa asked 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "It is a house above the seven heavens, beneath the Throne, called al-Darih." Al-Hasan said: the frequented House is the Ka'bah, which Allah causes to be visited every year by six hundred thousand, and if people fail to do so, Allah completes it with angels.

*Al-Saqf al-Marfu'* (the raised canopy): it is the heaven. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Throne, and it is the ceiling of Paradise.

*Al-Bahr al-Masjur* (the sea set aflame): Mujahid, Shimr ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Akhfash said: it is the sea kindled with fire. It is also narrated that the sea is Hell. Qatadah said: *al-masjur* means "filled." This is well known in the language, and al-Tabari preferred it, on the basis that the water of the sea is indeed like that. It does not contradict what Mujahid said, because *sajarta al-tannur* means: you filled the oven with what burns. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masjur* is that whose water has gone away. Dhu al-Rummah has no narration except this one, so it is one of the words with contrary meanings (al-adda'). It is narrated that the seas' water will go away on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas also said: *al-masjur* is the restrained, from which comes *sajur al-kalb*, the dog's collar of wood or iron that holds it back; and were it not that the sea is held back, it would overflow onto the earth. Al-Rabi' said: *al-masjur* is the mixture of sweet water with salt water. It is also said: *al-mafjur* (the burst), and this is supported by: ﴿And when the seas are burst open﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. Qutaybah ibn Sa'id said: it is Hell, and it was called a sea because of its vastness and its waves, as is said of the horse: "And if we find it truly a sea." These places were honored for these reasons. The oath by the inscribed Book is because the prophets (peace be upon them) had speech with Allah in these places, and its being coupled with the Tur indicates this. The oath by the raised canopy is to show the elevation of the frequented House. End.

I found him reciting in the Maghrib prayer: ﴿By the Tur﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is certain to befall, none can avert it﴾, and it was as if my heart was split open. So I embraced Islam out of fear of the descent of the punishment, and I did not think I would rise from my place before the punishment would befall me." Zayd ibn 'Ali recited *waqi'un* without the lam. Qatadah said: he means the punishment of the Hereafter for the disbelievers, i.e., it is certain to befall upon the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verse 23–28 (part 1 of 2):

Among the strange things that are related is that a man saw in a dream that on his palm were written five waws (واو). He was interpreted for with good, so he asked Ibn Sirin, and he said: "Prepare yourself for what will not please you." He said to him: "From where did you take this?" He said: "From the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿By the Mount (al-Tur)﴾ [al-Tur: 1] up to ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to occur﴾ [al-Tur: 7]." Not two or three days passed before that man was overtaken by that calamity.

Yawm (day) is governed by "dafi'" (repeller), as al-Hawfi said. Makki said: "It is not governed by waqi'," and he did not mention a proof for the prohibition. It was also said: it is in the accusative governed by His words "la-waqi'" (indeed it will occur), and it is appropriate that ﴿Nothing can repel it﴾ [al-Tur: 8] in this case be a parenthetical clause (jumlat i'tiradh) between the governing word and the governed.

Ibn 'Abbas said: (tamur) means "it trembles." He also said: "it splits." al-Dahhak said: "some of it surges into others." Mujahid said: "it revolves."

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]; this is at the beginning of the matter, then they are blown away until at the end they become ﴿like wool, fluffed up﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. (Fa-wayl) is conjoined to a sentence that contains the binding and emphasis of the meaning. And al-khawd (immersion) is floundering in falsehood, and its usage became predominant for plunging headlong into falsehood.

﴿The Day they will be pushed﴾ [al-Tur: 13]. That is because the guards of Hell shackle the hands of the disbelievers to their necks, gather their forelocks to their feet, and push them into the Fire, thrusting them on their faces and shoving them in the back of their necks. 'Ali, Abu Raja', al-Sulami and Zayd ibn 'Ali read: yud'awna, with a sukun on the dal and a fatha on the 'ayn, from al-du'a' (calling), meaning: it is said to them, "Come along to the Fire, and enter it." (Da'ann) means: being pushed, and it is said to them: ﴿This is the Fire﴾ [al-Tur: 14], when it has been said to them that, then after that they stood before the two aspects in which doubt can enter as to whether it is the Fire: either it is a magic that disguises the very essence of what is seen, or there is a defect in the viewer's sight. So He commanded them to burn in it, by way of rebuke. Then it was said to them, cutting off their hope: ﴿Whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you﴾ [al-Tur: 16]: your punishment is decreed, so your patience and your impatience are the same; there is no escape from the recompense of your deeds. Thus said Ibn 'Atiyya.

(p-148) al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ [al-Tur: 15], meaning: you used to say of the revelation, "This is magic."
﴿Is this magic?﴾ [al-Tur: 15], meaning: is this fulfilment also magic? The fa' has entered for this meaning.
﴿Or do you not see?﴾ [al-Tur: 15]: as you did not see in the world; meaning: or are you blind to what is reported, as you were blind to the news? This is rebuke and mockery. If you ask: why did He give as the reason for the equality or non-equality of patience the words ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [al-Tur: 16]? I say: because patience has a merit over impatience only for its benefit in the outcome, and because the patient one is recompensed with good. As for patience under punishment, which is itself the recompense and has no outcome or benefit, it has no merit over impatience. End of quotation. (Sihr) is the predicate, placed first; (hadha) is the subject; (sawa') is the subject, and the predicate is omitted, meaning patience and impatience. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning your patience and your abandoning of it are the same.

When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He mentioned the state of the believers, so that both warning and encouragement would occur; this is information about what the state of the believers will come to, and they were informed of it. It is also permissible that it is part of what is said to the disbelievers, since it adds to their grief and distress; the first is more apparent. The majority read: fakihin, in the accusative as a state and as the predicate regarding ﴿in gardens and bounty﴾ [al-Tur: 17]. Khalid read it in the nominative, as the predicate of inna, with fi jannat being related to it. Whoever permits multiple predicates permits that both be predicates. (Wa-waqahum) is conjoined to ﴿in gardens﴾ [al-Tur: 17], since the meaning is: they settled in gardens; or it is conjoined to (atahum), and ma is a verbal-noun particle, meaning: joyful by their Lord's giving them bounty and His protecting them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire. It has been permitted that the waw in (wa-waqahum) is the waw of circumstance, and whoever stipulates qad with the past tense says: here it is implied, meaning and indeed He had protected them. Abu Haywa read: wa-waqahum, with the qaf doubled.

﴿Eat and drink﴾ [al-Tur: 19] by supposing a verb of saying: meaning, it is said to them: (hani'an) (wholesome). al-Zamakhshari said: eating and drinking wholesomely, or food and drink wholesomely, which is that in which there is no disturbance. It is also permissible that it is like his saying:

Wholesome, pleasant, free of any hidden disease, for a glory from our honour that it has made lawful.

I mean: it is an adjective used in the manner of a verbal noun standing in place of the verb, raising what has made lawful, just as a verb raises it, as if it were said: here is the glory of the one who makes lawful our honour. Likewise the meaning of (hani'an) here: eating and drinking has made you content, or what you used to do has made you content, meaning the reward of what you used to do; the ba' is extra, as in (kafa billah), and the ba' is related to "eat and drink" if you make the agent the eating and drinking. End of quotation. We have previously discussed (hani'an) at length in Surat al-Nisa'. As for his permitting the extra ba', its addition is not analogical in the agent except in the agent of kafa, with disagreement about it; so permitting its addition in the agent here is not valid. As for his saying that the ba' is related to "eat and drink," this is not correct except for the actions, so it is related to one of them. (Muttaki'in) is in the accusative as a circumstance. Abu al-Baqa' said: from the pronoun in (kulu), or from the pronoun in (wa-waqahum), or from the pronoun in (atahum), or from the pronoun in (fakihin), or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase. End of quotation. The apparent view is that it is a circumstance of the adverbial phrase, which is His saying ﴿in gardens﴾ [al-Tur: 17]. Abu al-Samal read: 'ala sururin, with a fatha on the ra', which is a dialect of Kalb in the doubled form, to avoid a sequence of two dammas with doubling. 'Ikrima read: ﴿with wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] in the genitive construction.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And those who believed﴾ [al-Tur: 21] is the subject, and its predicate is (alhaqnahu). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (wa-alladhina) be in the accusative position, with the implied sense: "and We honoured those who believed." The meaning of the verse, said the majority, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and others, is that the believers whose descendants followed them in faith will be in the ranks of their fathers, even if they are not like them in piety and deeds, out of honour for their fathers. So bi-iman is related to His words ﴿and We made their descendants follow them﴾ [al-Qasas: 42]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the descendants of a believer to be with him in his rank, even if they did not reach it by their deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them." Then he recited the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: Allah the Exalted joins the young children to the believing fathers' rulings, even if they have not reached faith. End of quotation. So bi-iman is related to (alhaqna), meaning: by means of faith We joined the fathers with their descendants, namely the young ones who died before reaching the age of obligation; so they are in Paradise with their fathers. If the children of the disbelievers, who did not reach the limit of obligation, are in Paradise, as is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, then the children of believers are more deserving of it. al-Hasan said: the verse refers to the adult descendants. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it refers to the young ones, not the adults. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: "those who believed" are the Emigrants and the Helpers, and "the descendants" are the Successors. Also from him: if the fathers are of higher rank, Allah raises the sons up to them, so the fathers are included in the term "descendants." al-Nakha'i said: the meaning is: We gave them their rewards without any deficiency, and made their descendants likewise.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And those who believed﴾ [al-Tur: 21] is conjoined to "wide-eyed houris"; that is, We paired them with the wide-eyed houris, and with those who believed, that is, with their companions and fellows from among them, as in His words ﴿as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]. So they enjoy sometimes the playfulness of the houris, and sometimes the companionship of the believing brothers; and We made their descendants follow them. Then he mentioned the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, then said: so Allah gathers for them kinds of joy: in their own felicity, in the marriage with the wide-eyed houris, in the companionship of believing brothers, and in the gathering of their children and offspring with them. Then he said: ﴿With faith, We joined their descendants to them﴾: that is, by means of a great faith of lofty station, which is the faith of the fathers, We joined their descendants to their ranks, even though they do not merit them, as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, so that We complete their joy and perfect their bliss. If you ask: what is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "faith"? I say: its meaning is to indicate that it is a special faith of great rank. It is also permissible that what is meant is the faith of the descendants, of lower station, as if He said: with some faith which does not qualify them for the rank of their fathers, We joined them to them. End of quotation.

No one imagines that (wa-alladhina) is conjoined to ﴿wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] except this man, and that is a non-Arab imagination contrary to the understanding of the pure Arab Ibn 'Abbas and others. The best of these opinions is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and the hadith he narrated supports it, because the verses all describe Allah's bounty toward the people of Paradise. Among the parts of His bounty is that He shelters the doer of good in the wrongdoer. And the word ﴿We joined﴾ [al-Tur: 21] implies that the one joined has some shortcoming in deeds. Abu 'Amr read: wa-atba'nahum; the rest of the Seven: wa-attaba'at-hum; Abu 'Amr: "dhurriyyatihim" in the plural accusative; Ibn 'Amir: in the plural nominative; the rest of the Seven: in the singular; Ibn Jubayr: wa-atba'nahum dhurriyyatahum, with madd and hamza.

The majority read: ﴿alatnahum﴾ [al-Tur: 21], with a fatha on the lam, from alat; al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir: with a kasra on it; Ibn Hurmuz: aaltnahum, with madd, from alta, on the pattern af'ala; Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy: litnahum, from lat, which is the reading of Talha and al-A'mash; it was transmitted from Shibl and Ibn Kathir, and from Talha and al-A'mash also: latnahum with a fatha on the lam. Sahl said: a fatha on the lam without an alif is not permissible under any circumstances, and he also denied aaltnahum with madd, saying: it is not transmitted from anyone, and neither tafsir nor Arabic supports it; and this is not as he said, rather the lexicographers have reported alta with madd, as Ibn Hurmuz read. It was also read: wa-ma waltnahum, mentioned by Ibn Harun. Ibn Khalawayh said: so the root here is from lat yalit, and walat yalit, and alat ya'lit, and alat ya'lit and yu'lit, all of which mean "to diminish." It is also said that alat means "to become harsh." A man stood up before 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and admonished him, so a man said: "Do not harden (la ta'lit) the Commander of the Faithful," meaning: do not be harsh toward him. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "alatnahum" refers to the believers. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, joins the one who falls short to the one who does good, and does not diminish anything from the reward of the doer of good; this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and the majority. Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the children.

﴿From their deed﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, good and bad. This possibility is strengthened by His words ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, mortgaged to it. ﴿And We provided them﴾ [al-Tur: 22]: that is, We facilitated for them, little by little, continuously, without interruption.

﴿They pass around therein﴾: that is, they hand it to one another. al-Akhtal said:

I took from him the pure, mature wine, while the rooster crowed and the hour of the night-traveller arrived.

Or ﴿they pass around﴾: they pull at one another in playful pulling, since the people of the world find pleasure in that, and so too in Paradise. The majority read: ﴿No idle talk therein, nor any sinfulness﴾, with both in the nominative; Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with a fatha. Idle talk (laghw) is the empty speech that goes on between drinkers of wine in the world. Sinfulness (ta'thim) is the sin that befalls the drinker of wine in the world.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verses 23–28 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Youths of their own⁠⁠﴾: i.e., mamalik (slaves, servants). (Maknun): i.e., in the shell, untouched by hands, as said by Ibn Jubayr, and it is then fresh, so it is the finest and purest. It is also permissible that what is meant by "maknun" is "makhzun" (stored away), because only what is of high value is stored away. He said: "From the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿By the Mount (al-Tur)﴾ [al-Tur: 1] up to ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to occur﴾ [al-Tur: 7]." Not two or three days passed before that man was overtaken by that calamity.

Yawm (day) is governed by "dafi'" (repeller), as al-Hawfi said. Makki said: "It is not governed by waqi'," and he did not mention a proof for the prohibition. It was also said: it is in the accusative governed by His words "la-waqi'" (indeed it will occur), and it is appropriate that ﴿Nothing can repel it﴾ [al-Tur: 8] in this case be a parenthetical clause (jumlat i'tiradh) between the governing word and the governed.

Ibn 'Abbas said: (tamur) means "it trembles." He also said: "it splits." al-Dahhak said: "some of it surges into others." Mujahid said: "it revolves."

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]; this is at the beginning of the matter, then they are blown away until at the end they become ﴿like wool, fluffed up﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. (Fa-wayl) is conjoined to a sentence that contains the binding and emphasis of the meaning. And al-khawd (immersion) is floundering in falsehood, and its usage became predominant for plunging headlong into falsehood.

﴿The Day they will be pushed﴾ [al-Tur: 13]. That is because the guards of Hell shackle the hands of the disbelievers to their necks, gather their forelocks to their feet, and push them into the Fire, thrusting them on their faces and shoving them in the back of their necks. 'Ali, Abu Raja', al-Sulami and Zayd ibn 'Ali read: yud'awna, with a sukun on the dal and a fatha on the 'ayn, from al-du'a' (calling), meaning: it is said to them, "Come along to the Fire, and enter it." (Da'ann) means: being pushed, and it is said to them: ﴿This is the Fire﴾ [al-Tur: 14], when it has been said to them that, then after that they stood before the two aspects in which doubt can enter as to whether it is the Fire: either it is a magic that disguises the very essence of what is seen, or there is a defect in the viewer's sight. So He commanded them to burn in it, by way of rebuke. Then it was said to them, cutting off their hope: ﴿Whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you﴾ [al-Tur: 16]: your punishment is decreed, so your patience and your impatience are the same; there is no escape from the recompense of your deeds. Thus said Ibn 'Atiyya.

﴿Is this magic?﴾ [al-Tur: 15], meaning: is this fulfilment also magic? The fa' has entered for this meaning.
﴿Or do you not see?﴾ [al-Tur: 15]: as you did not see in the world; meaning: or are you blind to what is reported, as you were blind to the news? This is rebuke and mockery. If you ask: why did He give as the reason for the equality or non-equality of patience the words ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [al-Tur: 16]? I say: because patience has a merit over impatience only for its benefit in the outcome, and because the patient one is recompensed with good. As for patience under punishment, which is itself the recompense and has no outcome or benefit, it has no merit over impatience. End of quotation. (Sihr) is the predicate, placed first; (hadha) is the subject; (sawa') is the subject, and the predicate is omitted, meaning patience and impatience. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning your patience and your abandoning of it are the same.

When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He mentioned the state of the believers, so that both warning and encouragement would occur; this is information about what the state of the believers will come to, and they were informed of it. It is also permissible that it is part of what is said to the disbelievers, since it adds to their grief and distress; the first is more apparent. The majority read: fakihin, in the accusative as a state and as the predicate regarding ﴿in gardens and bounty﴾ [al-Tur: 17]. Khalid read it in the nominative, as the predicate of inna, with fi jannat being related to it. Whoever permits multiple predicates permits that both be predicates. It has been permitted that the waw in (wa-waqahum) is the waw of circumstance, and whoever stipulates qad with the past tense says: here it is implied, meaning and indeed He had protected them. Abu Haywa read: wa-waqahum, with the qaf doubled.

Wholesome, pleasant, free of any hidden disease, for a glory from our honour that it has made lawful.

I mean: it is an adjective used in the manner of a verbal noun standing in place of the verb, raising what has made lawful, just as a verb raises it, as if it were said: here is the glory of the one who makes lawful our honour. Likewise the meaning of (hani'an) here: eating and drinking has made you content, or what you used to do has made you content, meaning the reward of what you used to do; the ba' is extra, as in (kafa billah), and the ba' is related to "eat and drink" if you make the agent the eating and drinking. As for his saying that the ba' is related to "eat and drink," this is not correct except for the actions, so it is related to one of them. (Muttaki'in) is in the accusative as a circumstance. Abu al-Baqa' said: from the pronoun in (kulu), or from the pronoun in (wa-waqahum), or from the pronoun in (atahum), or from the pronoun in (fakihin), or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase. Abu al-Samal read: 'ala sururin, with a fatha on the ra', which is a dialect of Kalb in the doubled form, to avoid a sequence of two dammas with doubling. 'Ikrima read: ﴿with wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] in the genitive construction.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (wa-alladhina) be in the accusative position, with the implied sense: "and We honoured those who believed." The meaning of the verse, said the majority, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and others, is that the believers whose descendants followed them in faith will be in the ranks of their fathers, even if they are not like them in piety and deeds, out of honour for their fathers. So bi-iman is related to His words ﴿and We made their descendants follow them﴾ [al-Qasas: 42]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the descendants of a believer to be with him in his rank, even if they did not reach it by their deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them." Then he recited the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: Allah the Exalted joins the young children to the believing fathers' rulings, even if they have not reached faith. End of quotation. So bi-iman is related to (alhaqna), meaning: by means of faith We joined the fathers with their descendants, namely the young ones who died before reaching the age of obligation; so they are in Paradise with their fathers. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it refers to the young ones, not the adults. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: "those who believed" are the Emigrants and the Helpers, and "the descendants" are the Successors. Also from him: if the fathers are of higher rank, Allah raises the sons up to them, so the fathers are included in the term "descendants." al-Nakha'i said: the meaning is: We gave them their rewards without any deficiency, and made their descendants likewise.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And those who believed﴾ [al-Tur: 21] is conjoined to "wide-eyed houris"; that is, We paired them with the wide-eyed houris, and with those who believed, that is, with their companions and fellows from among them, as in His words ﴿as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]. So they enjoy sometimes the playfulness of the houris, and sometimes the companionship of the believing brothers; and We made their descendants follow them. Then he mentioned the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, then said: so Allah gathers for them kinds of joy: in their own felicity, in the marriage with the wide-eyed houris, in the companionship of believing brothers, and in the gathering of their children and offspring with them. Then he said: ﴿With faith, We joined their descendants to them﴾: that is, by means of a great faith of lofty station, which is the faith of the fathers, We joined their descendants to their ranks, even though they do not merit them, as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, so that We complete their joy and perfect their bliss. If you ask: what is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "faith"? I say: its meaning is to indicate that it is a special faith of great rank. It is also permissible that what is meant is the faith of the descendants, of lower station, as if He said: with some faith which does not qualify them for the rank of their fathers, We joined them to them. End of quotation.

No one imagines that (wa-alladhina) is conjoined to ﴿wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] except this man, and that is a non-Arab imagination contrary to the understanding of the pure Arab Ibn 'Abbas and others. The best of these opinions is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and the hadith he narrated supports it, because the verses all describe Allah's bounty toward the people of Paradise. Among the parts of His bounty is that He shelters the doer of good in the wrongdoer. And the word ﴿We joined﴾ [al-Tur: 21] implies that the one joined has some shortcoming in deeds. Abu 'Amr read: wa-atba'nahum; the rest of the Seven: wa-attaba'at-hum; Abu 'Amr: "dhurriyyatihim" in the plural accusative; Ibn 'Amir: in the plural nominative; the rest of the Seven: in the singular; Ibn Jubayr: wa-atba'nahum dhurriyyatahum, with madd and hamza.

The majority read: ﴿alatnahum﴾ [al-Tur: 21], with a fatha on the lam, from alat; al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir: with a kasra on it; Ibn Hurmuz: aaltnahum, with madd, from alta, on the pattern af'ala; Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy: litnahum, from lat, which is the reading of Talha and al-A'mash; it was transmitted from Shibl and Ibn Kathir, and from Talha and al-A'mash also: latnahum with a fatha on the lam. Sahl said: a fatha on the lam without an alif is not permissible under any circumstances, and he also denied aaltnahum with madd, saying: it is not transmitted from anyone, and neither tafsir nor Arabic supports it; and this is not as he said, rather the lexicographers have reported alta with madd, as Ibn Hurmuz read. It was also read: wa-ma waltnahum, mentioned by Ibn Harun. Ibn Khalawayh said: so the root here is from lat yalit, and walat yalit, and alat ya'lit, and alat ya'lit and yu'lit, all of which mean "to diminish." It is also said that alat means "to become harsh." A man stood up before 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and admonished him, so a man said: "Do not harden (la ta'lit) the Commander of the Faithful," meaning: do not be harsh toward him. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "alatnahum" refers to the believers. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, joins the one who falls short to the one who does good, and does not diminish anything from the reward of the doer of good; this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and the majority. Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the children.

﴿From their deed﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, good and bad. This possibility is strengthened by His words ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, mortgaged to it. ﴿And We provided them﴾ [al-Tur: 22]: that is, We facilitated for them, little by little, continuously, without interruption.

﴿They pass around therein﴾: that is, they hand it to one another. al-Akhtal said:

I took from him the pure, mature wine, while the rooster crowed and the hour of the night-traveller arrived.

Or ﴿they pass around﴾: they pull at one another in playful pulling, since the people of the world find pleasure in that, and so too in Paradise. The majority read: ﴿No idle talk therein, nor any sinfulness﴾, with both in the nominative; Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with a fatha. Idle talk (laghw) is the empty speech that goes on between drinkers of wine in the world. Sinfulness (ta'thim) is the sin that befalls the drinker of wine in the world.

Abu al-Samal read: 'ala sururin, with a fatha on the ra', which is a dialect of Kalb in the doubled form, to avoid a sequence of two dammas with doubling. 'Ikrima read: ﴿with wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] in the genitive construction.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And those who believed﴾ [al-Tur: 21] is the subject, and its predicate is (alhaqnahu). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (wa-alladhina) be in the accusative position, with the implied sense: "and We honoured those who believed." The meaning of the verse, said the majority, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and others, is that the believers whose descendants followed them in faith will be in the ranks of their fathers, even if they are not like them in piety and deeds, out of honour for their fathers. So bi-iman is related to His words ﴿and We made their descendants follow them﴾ [al-Qasas: 42]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the descendants of a believer to be with him in his rank, even if they did not reach it by their deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them." Then he recited the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: Allah the Exalted joins the young children to the believing fathers' rulings, even if they have not reached faith. End of quotation. So bi-iman is related to (alhaqna), meaning: by means of faith We joined the fathers with their descendants, namely the young ones who died before reaching the age of obligation; so they are in Paradise with their fathers. If the children of the disbelievers, who did not reach the limit of obligation, are in Paradise, as is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, then the children of believers are more deserving of it. al-Hasan said: the verse refers to the adult descendants. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it refers to the young ones, not the adults. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: "those who believed" are the Emigrants and the Helpers, and "the descendants" are the Successors. Also from him: if the fathers are of higher rank, Allah raises the sons up to them, so the fathers are included in the term "descendants." al-Nakha'i said: the meaning is: We gave them their rewards without any deficiency, and made their descendants likewise.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And those who believed﴾ [al-Tur: 21] is conjoined to "wide-eyed houris"; that is, We paired them with the wide-eyed houris, and with those who believed, that is, with their companions and fellows from among them, as in His words ﴿as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]. So they enjoy sometimes the playfulness of the houris, and sometimes the companionship of the believing brothers; and We made their descendants follow them. Then he mentioned the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, then said: so Allah gathers for them kinds of joy: in their own felicity, in the marriage with the wide-eyed houris, in the companionship of believing brothers, and in the gathering of their children and offspring with them. Then he said: ﴿With faith, We joined their descendants to them﴾: that is, by means of a great faith of lofty station, which is the faith of the fathers, We joined their descendants to their ranks, even though they do not merit them, as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, so that We complete their joy and perfect their bliss. If you ask: what is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "faith"? I say: its meaning is to indicate that it is a special faith of great rank. It is also permissible that what is meant is the faith of the descendants, of lower station, as if He said: with some faith which does not qualify them for the rank of their fathers, We joined them to them. End of quotation.

No one imagines that (wa-alladhina) is conjoined to ﴿wide-eyed houris﴾ [al-Tur: 20] except this man, and that is a non-Arab imagination contrary to the understanding of the pure Arab Ibn 'Abbas and others. The best of these opinions is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and the hadith he narrated supports it, because the verses all describe Allah's bounty toward the people of Paradise. Among the parts of His bounty is that He shelters the doer of good in the wrongdoer. And the word ﴿We joined﴾ [al-Tur: 21] implies that the one joined has some shortcoming in deeds. Abu 'Amr read: wa-atba'nahum; the rest of the Seven: wa-attaba'at-hum; Abu 'Amr: "dhurriyyatihim" in the plural accusative; Ibn 'Amir: in the plural nominative; the rest of the Seven: in the singular; Ibn Jubayr: wa-atba'nahum dhurriyyatahum, with madd and hamza.

The majority read: ﴿alatnahum﴾ [al-Tur: 21], with a fatha on the lam, from alat; al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir: with a kasra on it; Ibn Hurmuz: aaltnahum, with madd, from alta, on the pattern af'ala; Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy: litnahum, from lat, which is the reading of Talha and al-A'mash; it was transmitted from Shibl and Ibn Kathir, and from Talha and al-A'mash also: latnahum with a fatha on the lam. Sahl said: a fatha on the lam without an alif is not permissible under any circumstances, and he also denied aaltnahum with madd, saying: it is not transmitted from anyone, and neither tafsir nor Arabic supports it; and this is not as he said, rather the lexicographers have reported alta with madd, as Ibn Hurmuz read. It was also read: wa-ma waltnahum, mentioned by Ibn Harun. Ibn Khalawayh said: so the root here is from lat yalit, and walat yalit, and alat ya'lit, and alat ya'lit and yu'lit, all of which mean "to diminish." It is also said that alat means "to become harsh." A man stood up before 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and admonished him, so a man said: "Do not harden (la ta'lit) the Commander of the Faithful," meaning: do not be harsh toward him. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "alatnahum" refers to the believers. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, joins the one who falls short to the one who does good, and does not diminish anything from the reward of the doer of good; this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and the majority. Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the children.

﴿From their deed﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, good and bad. This possibility is strengthened by His words ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ [al-Tur: 21]: that is, mortgaged to it. ﴿And We provided them﴾ [al-Tur: 22]: that is, We facilitated for them, little by little, continuously, without interruption.

﴿They pass around therein﴾: that is, they hand it to one another. al-Akhtal said:

I took from him the pure, mature wine, while the rooster crowed and the hour of the night-traveller arrived.

Or ﴿they pass around﴾: they pull at one another in playful pulling, since the people of the world find pleasure in that, and so too in Paradise. The majority read: ﴿No idle talk therein, nor any sinfulness﴾, with both in the nominative; Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with a fatha. Idle talk (laghw) is the empty speech that goes on between drinkers of wine in the world. Sinfulness (ta'thim) is the sin that befalls the drinker of wine in the world.

﴿Nad'uhu﴾: we worship Him and ask Him for protection from His punishment. ﴿Innahu huwa al-barr﴾: the Benefactor (al-Muhsin), (al-Rahim): the One of abundant mercy; when He is worshipped He rewards, and when He is asked He responds. Ibn 'Abbas said: (tamur) means "it trembles." He also said: "it splits." al-Dahhak said: "some of it surges into others." Mujahid said: "it revolves."

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]; this is at the beginning of the matter, then they are blown away until at the end they become ﴿like wool, fluffed up﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. (Fa-wayl) is conjoined to a sentence that contains the binding and emphasis of the meaning. And al-khawd (immersion) is floundering in falsehood, and its usage became predominant for plunging headlong into falsehood.

﴿The Day they will be pushed﴾ [al-Tur: 13]. (Da'ann) means: being pushed, and it is said to them: ﴿This is the Fire﴾ [al-Tur: 14], when it has been said to them that, then after that they stood before the two aspects in which doubt can enter as to whether it is the Fire: either it is a magic that disguises the very essence of what is seen, or there is a defect in the viewer's sight. So He commanded them to burn in it, by way of rebuke. When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He mentioned the state of the believers, so that both warning and encouragement would occur; this is information about what the state of the believers will come to, and they were informed of it. It is also permissible that it is part of what is said to the disbelievers, since it adds to their grief and distress; the first is more apparent. (p-151) When God Almighty's oath concerning the occurrence of the punishment had preceded, and He had mentioned some matters concerning the circumstances of those who are punished and those who are saved, He commanded him to admonish, warning the disbeliever and giving good news to the believer, and calling to God by spreading His message. Then He negated from him what the disbelievers attributed to him of soothsaying (kihanah) and madness, since these two were ways of reporting some unseen matters, and the jinn had a connection with humans through them. Among those who attributed soothsaying to him was Shayba ibn Rabi'a, and among those who attributed madness to him was Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'So admonish' means: persist in reminding and advising people, and let not their saying 'a soothsayer' or 'a madman' discourage you; do not pay attention to it, for it is a false and self-contradictory statement. The soothsayer needs cleverness and keenness of perception in his soothsaying, while the madman has his intellect covered; and you, by the praise of God Most High and His bounty upon you, are neither of these two, but rather you have the truth of prophethood and the soundness of intellect." End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "'By the blessing of your Lord' is connected to what the speech indicates, and it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject of 'ma' and its predicate. The meaning is: you are not, in the state of your reminding by the blessing of your Lord, a soothsayer." Abu al-Baqa' said: "The ba' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of 'bi-kahin' or 'majnun' is the implied meaning. The sense is: you are not a soothsayer nor a madman, being connected with the blessing of your Lord." End of quote. It would be a permanent (lazimah) circumstantial clause, not a transient one, because he, upon him be prayer and peace, was always connected with the blessing of his Lord. It was also said: "By the blessing of your Lord" is an oath by it, as if it were said: "By the blessing of your Lord, you are not a soothsayer nor a madman." So the object of the oath is placed between the subject and the predicate, as you say: "Zayd is not, by God, standing."

When He negated from him soothsaying and madness, which some disbelievers attributed to him, He mentioned another type of what they were saying.

It is narrated that the Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (council house), and their opinions about him (ﷺ) multiplied, until one speaker among them, who were the Banu Abd al-Dar, said, as related by al-Dahhak: "Wait for him to meet the vicissitudes of fate, for he is a poet who will perish just as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." So they dispersed upon this statement, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The saying of whoever said this reflects a deficiency of natural disposition such that he does not perceive poetry, which is speech measured in a known pattern distinct from prose that is not on that course. Undoubtedly some of them did perceive this, since there were poets among them; but they colluded with those deficient in disposition in saying, "He is a poet," denying the signs of God after their certainty of them.

Zayd ibn Ali read "yutarabbas" with ya' in the passive form, and "rayb" as nominative. "Rayb al-manun" means the calamities of time, for it does not remain in one state. The poet said:

"Wait for her (the wife) the calamity of fate; perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die."

And al-Hindi said:

"Do you lament from fate and its calamity? And time does not reproach whoever despairs."

"Say: wait": this is an imperative of threat, from those who wait for your destruction, just as you wait for my destruction.

"Do their minds command them to this?" Their intellects, with this, i.e., with their saying "soothsayer," "poet," and "madman," which is a self-contradictory statement. The Quraysh were called the people of intellect and understanding. It was said to Amr ibn al-As: "What is the matter with your people, that they did not believe, when God Most High has described them as having intellect?" He said: "Those are intellects that God has outwitted," meaning that success (tawfiq) did not accompany them.

"Or does their intellect command them": it was said that "am" here has the meaning of the interrogative hamzah, i.e., "Does their intellect command them?" Mujahid interpreted it as "bal" (rather), and the correct view is that it can be interpreted as both "bal" and the hamzah.

"Or are they a transgressing people": i.e., those who exceed the limit in obstinacy despite the manifestation of truth. Mujahid read "bal hum" in place of "am hum." The attribution of commanding to intellects is metaphorical, since when they led to that, they were treated as commanding, as in His saying: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped?" (Hud: 87). Al-Tha'labi related from al-Khalil that he said: "Every 'am' in Surat al-Tur is interrogative and not conjunctive."

"Taqawwalahu" means he fabricated it from his own self, as He said: "And if he had invented against Us some sayings" (al-Haqqah: 44). Ibn Atiyya said: "Taqawwalahu" means: he said that it was said by another; it is an expression for a specific lie. End of quote.

"Rather, they do not believe": i.e., because of their disbelief and obstinacy. Then He challenged them with His saying: "Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful": i.e., one similar to the Qur'an in its composition and arrangement, in eloquence, soundness of meanings, reports of the stories of past nations and of unseen matters. The ruling is: if they are truthful that he fabricated it, then let them say something like it, since he is one of them; so if they are truthful, let them be like him in fabricating. Al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read "bi-hadithin mithlihi" with the construct form, meaning: with the speech of a man like the Messenger in being unlettered (ummi), who did not accompany the people of knowledge nor travelled from his land; or like him in being one of them; so it is not permissible that there be anyone like him among the Arabs in eloquence. So let them bring something like what he brought, and they will never be able to do that.

"Or were they created from nothing": i.e., from nothing living like inanimate matter, so they are not commanded nor forbidden, as inanimate things are. Al-Tabari said this. It was also said: "from nothing" means: without a cause nor for the purpose of punishment or reward, so they therefore do not listen nor accept law. This is like your saying: "I did such and such without a cause," meaning "for no cause," so "min" here is causal, while in the first view it indicates the starting point.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or were they created': or were they brought into existence and measured with the measure upon which their nature is based; 'from nothing': from no measurer. Or are they the ones who created themselves, since they do not worship the Creator? 'Rather, they do not have certainty': i.e., if they are asked, 'Who created you and created the heavens and the earth?' they say, 'God,' while they doubt what they say and are not certain. Or were they created without a Lord and without a creator? I.e., or were they brought into existence and emerged into being without a god who makes them emerge and brings them into being? 'Or are they the creators' of themselves, so that they worship God and not obey His commands and not refrain from His prohibitions? Both alternatives are false, and they acknowledge that, so that proves their falsehood." Ibn Atiyya said: "Then He placed them in a position of rebuke concerning themselves: Are they the ones who created things, so that they are arrogant because of that? Then He specified among those things the heavens and the earth, for their greatness and nobility among created things. Then He judged against them that they do not have certainty and do not look in a way that leads them to certainty."

"Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?" Al-Zamakhshari said: The treasuries of provision, so that they might bestow prophethood upon whomever they wish? Or: Do they have the treasuries of His knowledge, so that they might choose for it whomever they wish, with wisdom and benefit? "Or are they the controllers": the lords who dominate, so that they could manage the affair of lordship and build matters upon their will. Ibn Atiyya said: "Or do they have independence from God Most High in all affairs, since wealth, health, strength and other things are all from the treasuries of God Most High?" Al-Zahrawi said: "It was said that by the treasuries He means knowledge, and this is a good view if considered and expanded." Al-Rummani said: "His treasuries, Exalted is He, are His capabilities." End of quote. "Al-musaytir," Ibn Abbas said: "the one who is empowered, the dominant." The majority read "al-musaytirun" with the sad; Hisham, Qunbul, and Hafs, according to one narration from him, read it with the sin, which is the original; and whoever substituted it with a sad did so because of the letter of elevation (isti'la'), which is the ta'. Khallad from Hamza, and Khallad from him, according to one narration from him, gave it the sound of the zay (ishmam).

"Or do they have a ladder" set up to the heaven, "upon which they listen": i.e., upon it or from it, since prepositions may take the place of one another. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ascending upon it." The object of "yastami'un" is omitted; its estimate is: the news of the correctness of what they claim. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: what is revealed to the angels of knowledge of the unseen, so that they might know what will occur, such as the prior destruction of Muhammad (ﷺ) before their destruction, and his victory in the end over them, as they claim.

"Then let their listener bring a clear authority": i.e., a clear proof of the truthfulness of their listening to the one who listens to them. "Or do you ask them for a reward," for belief in God, His unity, and following His law, "so they are burdened with heavy debt": that heavy, binding burden, which prompted their aversion to following you.

"Or do they have the unseen, so that they write": i.e., the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), "so that they write": i.e., they establish that for people as law, which is worship of idols, dedicating camels (tasyib al-sawa'ib), and other such practices of theirs. It was also said: the meaning is: they know when Muhammad (ﷺ), whom they await for, will die; and "write" means: they judge. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: do they have the Preserved Tablet, so that they write what is in it and report it?"

"Or do they intend a scheme": i.e., against you and your law; this is their scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa. "But those who disbelieved": i.e., they; the apparent noun is used to draw attention to the cause, or "those who disbelieved" is general, so they are included in it. "They are the ones who will be ensnared": i.e., those upon whom the consequence of their scheme returns, and whose plotting encircles them. That is because they were killed on the day of Badr, and He named their defeat a "scheme," since it was the punishment for scheming.

"Or do they have a god other than God" to protect them and defend them against the onset of their destruction? Then He declared Himself free: "Exalted is God above what they associate": with idols and images.

"And if they see a fragment of the sky falling": the Quraysh had proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among what they proposed, their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim" (al-Isra': 92). So He informed that if they saw that directly, according to their proposal, their insolence and ignorance would drive them to deceive themselves about what they witnessed, and they would say: "It is a gathered cloud," piled up, one part upon another, raining upon us, and not a fragment falling as punishment.

"So leave them": an imperative of truce, abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. The majority read "until they meet their day"; Abu Haywa read "hatta yalqawu," the imperfect of laqiya. "Their day": i.e., the day of their death one by one. The "sa'q" (stunning) is punishment; or the day of Badr, since they were punished on it; or the Day of Resurrection, these are views, and the third is the view of the majority, since His stunning encompasses all creatures. The majority read "yusa'qun" with a fatha on the ya'. 'Asim, Ibn Amir, Zayd ibn Ali and the people of Mecca read it [in the saying of Shibl ibn Ubada], and the people of Mecca opened it, as the majority did in the saying of Isma'il. Al-Sulami read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the 'ayn, from the quadriliteral "asa'qa."

"And indeed for those who did wrong": i.e., for these wrongdoers, "a punishment short of that": i.e., short of the Day of Resurrection and before it, which is the day of Badr and the conquest, as Ibn Abbas and others said. Al-Barra' ibn Azib and Ibn Abbas also said: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: their calamities in this world. Mujahid said: it is hunger and drought for seven years.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verses 29–49 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿فَإنَّكَ بِأعْيُنِنا﴾ ("Indeed, you are under Our eyes"): this is an expression for protection and safekeeping. It is in the plural ("eyes") because it is attached to a pronoun of plurality. When the pronoun is singular, the noun is given in the singular, as in Allah's words: ﴿ولِتُصْنَعَ عَلى عَيْنِي﴾ ("and that you may be raised under My eye") [Ta-Ha: 39]. Abu al-Sammal recited it as *bi-a'yunna* ("bi-a'yunnā"), with a single doubled nun.

﴿وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("and glorify your Lord with His praise") [Ta-Ha: 130]. Abu al-Ahwas Awf ibn Malik said: it is the well-known *tasbih*, which is saying "Subhan Allah" at every standing. Ata said: when you rise from every gathering. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Ibn Abbas said: when you rise from your sleep. It has also been said that it is the voluntary prayer, and it has been said that it is the obligatory prayer. Al-Dahhak said: when you rise to prayer, you say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You." Zayd ibn Aslam said: when you rise from the midday rest and the glorification, and that is the time of the noon prayer. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: remember Allah with your tongue when you rise from your bed until you enter into the prayer.

﴿ومِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ﴾ ("and glorify Him during part of the night"): before the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers.

﴿وإدْبارَ النُّجُومِ﴾ ("and at the retreat of the stars"): the Subh (dawn) prayer. It is related from Amr, Ali, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan that it refers to the voluntary prayers, and that *wa-idbar al-nujum* means the two rak'ahs of Fajr. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, al-Minhal ibn Amr and Ya'qub recited *wa-adbar* with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "and the aftermaths (the last parts) of the stars."
