**Surat al-Najm (The Star)** is Meccan, and it has sixty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. ﴿Your companion has neither strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2]. ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3]. ﴿It is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. ﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5]. ﴿Possessor of strength; and he stood firm﴾ [al-Najm: 6]. ﴿While he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7]. ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8]. ﴿And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9]. ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. ﴿The heart did not lie in what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11]. ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. ﴿And he had certainly seen him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13]. ﴿At the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14]. ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15]. ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. ﴿The gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19]. ﴿And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 20]. ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21]. ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [al-Najm: 22]. ﴿They are not but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow not except assumption and what the souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. ﴿Or will man have whatever he wishes?﴾ [al-Najm: 24]. ﴿For to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [al-Najm: 25]. ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not benefit at all, except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26]. ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with names of females﴾ [al-Najm: 27]. ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow not except assumption, and indeed assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28]. ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ [al-Najm: 30]. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they have done and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, other than minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He is most knowing of you, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers. So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾ [al-Najm: 33], ﴿and gave a little and then withheld﴾ [al-Najm: 34]? ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35]. ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾ [al-Najm: 36], ﴿and of Abraham who fulfilled [his trust]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]? ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38], ﴿and that man will have only what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], ﴿and that his effort will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 40], ﴿then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾ [al-Najm: 41], ﴿and that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm: 42], ﴿and that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ [al-Najm: 43], ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 44], ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female﴾ [al-Najm: 45], ﴿from a sperm-drop when it is emitted﴾ [al-Najm: 46], ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾ [al-Najm: 47], ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48], ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50], ﴿and Thamud, and spared none﴾ [al-Najm: 51], ﴿and the people of Noah before, for they were more unjust and more transgressive﴾ [al-Najm: 52], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿and covered them with what covered them﴾ [al-Najm: 54]. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute?﴾ [al-Najm: 55]. ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]. ﴿The approaching [Hour] has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]. ﴿None besides Allah can disclose it﴾ [al-Najm: 58]. ﴿Do you then wonder at this statement﴾ [al-Najm: 59], ﴿and laugh and not weep﴾ [al-Najm: 60], ﴿while you are proud [and heedless]?﴾ [al-Najm: 61]. ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [al-Najm: 62].

*Al-mirrah* means strength, from *amrartu al-habl*, when one twists the rope tightly. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of a man of sound judgment and sharp intellect that he is *dhu mirrah* ("possessor of strength"). He said:

> And I am one of firm strength, a bitter one [in the face of hardship],
> when a relative rides against my relative.

*Tadalla al-'idhq tadallayan* means that it stretched from a height down toward the bottom; it is used for nearness to the height. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi. Usama al-Hudhali said:

> It hung down over us, and it was a dove's blue-gray,
> when the moss at the end of the summer heat was dry.

*Al-qab* and *al-qayb*, and *al-qadah* and *al-qid*, mean a measure. *Al-qaws* (the bow) is well known; it is an instrument for shooting arrows, and its shapes vary. *Al-sidrah* is the lote tree (the jujube tree). *Al-dhiza* means unjust, from *dhaza-hu yadhiżu-hu*, when one oppresses him. The poet said:

> The Banu Asad were unjust in their judgment,
> when they made the head like the tail.

Its original form is *dhuzā* on the pattern *fu'lā*, like *hubla* and *unthā* and *ruyyā*. What happened to it is what happened to *bayyad* so that the *ya'* is preserved. A form *fi'lā* with a kasra on the first letter does not occur in adjectives, as Sibawayh said. Tha'lab reported *mishyatun jubkā* ("a walk of a particular kind") and *rajulun kīṣā*. Others reported *imra'atun 'izhā* and *imra'atun si'lā*, but the known forms are *'izmāh* and *si'lāh*. Al-Kisa'i said: *dāza yadīzu dīzā*, *dāza yadūzu dīwzā*, and *da'aza yad'azu di'zan*.

*Al-lamam* is what is small and slight. From it comes *al-lamam*, the touch of madness. *Alamma bi-l-makan* means he stayed in a place briefly; *alamma bi-l-ta'am* means he ate only a little of the food. Al-Mubarrad said: the root meaning of *al-lamam* is to approach something without actually engaging in it; one says *alamma bi-kadha*, meaning he came close to it without mixing with it. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs use *al-ilmam* for approaching and drawing near; one says *alamma yaf'alu kadha*, meaning he almost does it. Jarir said:

> My soul, the one whom he fends off is dear to me,
> and whose visit to me is a brief encounter.

Another said:

> The meeting of the friends at the rock is a brief encounter.

*Al-ajinnah* is the plural of *janin*, which is the child in the womb. It was named so because it is hidden. *Al-ijtinan* means concealment.

*Akda*: its origin is from *al-kudyah*. It is said of one who digs a well and then reaches a rock in which digging cannot proceed: "He has been stopped (*akda*)." Then the Arabs used it for one who gives but does not complete the giving, and for one who seeks something but does not reach its end. Al-Hutay'a said:

> He gave a little, then withheld his gift,
> and whoever spends kindness among people is praised.

Al-Kisa'i and others said: *akda al-hafir* means the digger reached a hard stone or a mountain and could not dig further. *Hafara fa-akda* means he dug and reached solid ground. It is also said: *kadiyat asabi'uhu* when his fingers grew tired from digging. *Kada al-bayt* means its income decreased. Abu Zayd said: *akda al-rajul* means his goodness decreased.

*Aqna*: al-Jawhari said: *qaniya yaqna qinan*, like *ghaniya yaghna ghinan*. It is transitive by changing the vowel, so one says *qaniytu al-mal*, meaning I acquired wealth, like *shatartu 'ayn al-rajul* and *shatara-hā Allah*. After that it became transitive by a hamza or by doubling, so one says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *qannāhu Allah mālan*. The poet said:

> How many a rich man has had his wealth struck by fate,
> and how many a poor man has acquired property after destitution.

That is, *taqanna al-mal*. One also says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *arḍāhu* ("He gave him property and contentment") from *al-qinyah*. Abu Zayd said: the Arabs say of one who is given a hundred goats: "He has been given *al-qina*"; of one given a hundred sheep: "He has been given *al-ghina*"; and of one given a hundred camels: "He has been given *al-muna*."

*Al-Shi'ra* is the bright star that rises after Orion (al-Jawza'), and its rising is in the intensity of heat. It is called "the pursuer of Orion." They are the two Shi'ras: the *'Ubur* which is in Orion, and the *Ghumayṣā'* (the Dog Star) which is in the forearm. The Arabs claim that they are the sisters of Suhayl. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also called the Dog of the Mighty One (*kalb al-jabbar*). They are two Shi'ras: al-Ghumayṣa' and al-'Ubur. Among the lies of the Arabs is that Suhayl and al-Shi'ra were a married couple; Suhayl descended and became a Yemeni, so al-Shi'ra pursued him, the 'Ubur, and she crossed the Milky Way, so she was called *al-'Ubur*; and the Ghumayṣā' stayed behind because she was less visible than the other.

*Azifa*: it drew near. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

> Youth has departed, and this gray hair has drawn near,
> and I see no departed youth coming back.

Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

> The departure has drawn near, but our saddles
> are still on our mounts, as if it were already.

It is also narrated as *afida al-tarahhul*.

*Samada*: he was heedless and played. The poet said:

> Surely you, O man, are heedless,
> as if you will never perish, and you are not destroyed.

Another said:

> It was said: "Rise, look at them,
> then leave aside the sumud."

Abu Ubayda said: *al-sumud* is singing in the language of Himyar. They say: "O girl, *usmudi* for us," meaning sing for us.

(p-151) When God Almighty's oath concerning the occurrence of the punishment had preceded, and He had mentioned some matters concerning the circumstances of those who are punished and those who are saved, He commanded him to admonish, warning the disbeliever and giving good news to the believer, and calling to God by spreading His message. Then He negated from him what the disbelievers attributed to him of soothsaying (kihanah) and madness, since these two were ways of reporting some unseen matters, and the jinn had a connection with humans through them. Among those who attributed soothsaying to him was Shayba ibn Rabi'a, and among those who attributed madness to him was Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'So admonish' means: persist in reminding and advising people, and let not their saying 'a soothsayer' or 'a madman' discourage you; do not pay attention to it, for it is a false and self-contradictory statement. The soothsayer needs cleverness and keenness of perception in his soothsaying, while the madman has his intellect covered; and you, by the praise of God Most High and His bounty upon you, are neither of these two, but rather you have the truth of prophethood and the soundness of intellect." End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "'By the blessing of your Lord' is connected to what the speech indicates, and it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject of 'ma' and its predicate. The meaning is: you are not, in the state of your reminding by the blessing of your Lord, a soothsayer." Abu al-Baqa' said: "The ba' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of 'bi-kahin' or 'majnun' is the implied meaning. The sense is: you are not a soothsayer nor a madman, being connected with the blessing of your Lord." End of quote. It would be a permanent (lazimah) circumstantial clause, not a transient one, because he, upon him be prayer and peace, was always connected with the blessing of his Lord. It was also said: "By the blessing of your Lord" is an oath by it, as if it were said: "By the blessing of your Lord, you are not a soothsayer nor a madman." So the object of the oath is placed between the subject and the predicate, as you say: "Zayd is not, by God, standing."

When He negated from him soothsaying and madness, which some disbelievers attributed to him, He mentioned another type of what they were saying.

It is narrated that the Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (council house), and their opinions about him (ﷺ) multiplied, until one speaker among them, who were the Banu Abd al-Dar, said, as related by al-Dahhak: "Wait for him to meet the vicissitudes of fate, for he is a poet who will perish just as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." So they dispersed upon this statement, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The saying of whoever said this reflects a deficiency of natural disposition such that he does not perceive poetry, which is speech measured in a known pattern distinct from prose that is not on that course. Undoubtedly some of them did perceive this, since there were poets among them; but they colluded with those deficient in disposition in saying, "He is a poet," denying the signs of God after their certainty of them.

Zayd ibn Ali read "yutarabbas" with ya' in the passive form, and "rayb" as nominative. "Rayb al-manun" means the calamities of time, for it does not remain in one state. The poet said:

"Wait for her (the wife) the calamity of fate; perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die."

And al-Hindi said:

"Do you lament from fate and its calamity? And time does not reproach whoever despairs."

"Say: wait": this is an imperative of threat, from those who wait for your destruction, just as you wait for my destruction.

"Do their minds command them to this?" Their intellects, with this, i.e., with their saying "soothsayer," "poet," and "madman," which is a self-contradictory statement. The Quraysh were called the people of intellect and understanding. It was said to Amr ibn al-As: "What is the matter with your people, that they did not believe, when God Most High has described them as having intellect?" He said: "Those are intellects that God has outwitted," meaning that success (tawfiq) did not accompany them.

"Or does their intellect command them": it was said that "am" here has the meaning of the interrogative hamzah, i.e., "Does their intellect command them?" Mujahid interpreted it as "bal" (rather), and the correct view is that it can be interpreted as both "bal" and the hamzah.

"Or are they a transgressing people": i.e., those who exceed the limit in obstinacy despite the manifestation of truth. Mujahid read "bal hum" in place of "am hum." The attribution of commanding to intellects is metaphorical, since when they led to that, they were treated as commanding, as in His saying: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped?" (Hud: 87). Al-Tha'labi related from al-Khalil that he said: "Every 'am' in Surat al-Tur is interrogative and not conjunctive."

"Taqawwalahu" means he fabricated it from his own self, as He said: "And if he had invented against Us some sayings" (al-Haqqah: 44). Ibn Atiyya said: "Taqawwalahu" means: he said that it was said by another; it is an expression for a specific lie. End of quote.

"Rather, they do not believe": i.e., because of their disbelief and obstinacy. Then He challenged them with His saying: "Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful": i.e., one similar to the Qur'an in its composition and arrangement, in eloquence, soundness of meanings, reports of the stories of past nations and of unseen matters. The ruling is: if they are truthful that he fabricated it, then let them say something like it, since he is one of them; so if they are truthful, let them be like him in fabricating. Al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read "bi-hadithin mithlihi" with the construct form, meaning: with the speech of a man like the Messenger in being unlettered (ummi), who did not accompany the people of knowledge nor travelled from his land; or like him in being one of them; so it is not permissible that there be anyone like him among the Arabs in eloquence. So let them bring something like what he brought, and they will never be able to do that.

"Or were they created from nothing": i.e., from nothing living like inanimate matter, so they are not commanded nor forbidden, as inanimate things are. Al-Tabari said this. It was also said: "from nothing" means: without a cause nor for the purpose of punishment or reward, so they therefore do not listen nor accept law. This is like your saying: "I did such and such without a cause," meaning "for no cause," so "min" here is causal, while in the first view it indicates the starting point.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or were they created': or were they brought into existence and measured with the measure upon which their nature is based; 'from nothing': from no measurer. Or are they the ones who created themselves, since they do not worship the Creator? 'Rather, they do not have certainty': i.e., if they are asked, 'Who created you and created the heavens and the earth?' they say, 'God,' while they doubt what they say and are not certain. Or were they created without a Lord and without a creator? I.e., or were they brought into existence and emerged into being without a god who makes them emerge and brings them into being? 'Or are they the creators' of themselves, so that they worship God and not obey His commands and not refrain from His prohibitions? Both alternatives are false, and they acknowledge that, so that proves their falsehood." Ibn Atiyya said: "Then He placed them in a position of rebuke concerning themselves: Are they the ones who created things, so that they are arrogant because of that? Then He specified among those things the heavens and the earth, for their greatness and nobility among created things. Then He judged against them that they do not have certainty and do not look in a way that leads them to certainty."

"Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?" Al-Zamakhshari said: The treasuries of provision, so that they might bestow prophethood upon whomever they wish? Or: Do they have the treasuries of His knowledge, so that they might choose for it whomever they wish, with wisdom and benefit? "Or are they the controllers": the lords who dominate, so that they could manage the affair of lordship and build matters upon their will. Ibn Atiyya said: "Or do they have independence from God Most High in all affairs, since wealth, health, strength and other things are all from the treasuries of God Most High?" Al-Zahrawi said: "It was said that by the treasuries He means knowledge, and this is a good view if considered and expanded." Al-Rummani said: "His treasuries, Exalted is He, are His capabilities." End of quote. "Al-musaytir," Ibn Abbas said: "the one who is empowered, the dominant." The majority read "al-musaytirun" with the sad; Hisham, Qunbul, and Hafs, according to one narration from him, read it with the sin, which is the original; and whoever substituted it with a sad did so because of the letter of elevation (isti'la'), which is the ta'. Khallad from Hamza, and Khallad from him, according to one narration from him, gave it the sound of the zay (ishmam).

"Or do they have a ladder" set up to the heaven, "upon which they listen": i.e., upon it or from it, since prepositions may take the place of one another. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ascending upon it." The object of "yastami'un" is omitted; its estimate is: the news of the correctness of what they claim. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: what is revealed to the angels of knowledge of the unseen, so that they might know what will occur, such as the prior destruction of Muhammad (ﷺ) before their destruction, and his victory in the end over them, as they claim.

"Then let their listener bring a clear authority": i.e., a clear proof of the truthfulness of their listening to the one who listens to them. "Or do you ask them for a reward," for belief in God, His unity, and following His law, "so they are burdened with heavy debt": that heavy, binding burden, which prompted their aversion to following you.

"Or do they have the unseen, so that they write": i.e., the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), "so that they write": i.e., they establish that for people as law, which is worship of idols, dedicating camels (tasyib al-sawa'ib), and other such practices of theirs. It was also said: the meaning is: they know when Muhammad (ﷺ), whom they await for, will die; and "write" means: they judge. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: do they have the Preserved Tablet, so that they write what is in it and report it?"

"Or do they intend a scheme": i.e., against you and your law; this is their scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa. "But those who disbelieved": i.e., they; the apparent noun is used to draw attention to the cause, or "those who disbelieved" is general, so they are included in it. "They are the ones who will be ensnared": i.e., those upon whom the consequence of their scheme returns, and whose plotting encircles them. That is because they were killed on the day of Badr, and He named their defeat a "scheme," since it was the punishment for scheming.

"Or do they have a god other than God" to protect them and defend them against the onset of their destruction? Then He declared Himself free: "Exalted is God above what they associate": with idols and images.

"And if they see a fragment of the sky falling": the Quraysh had proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among what they proposed, their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim" (al-Isra': 92). So He informed that if they saw that directly, according to their proposal, their insolence and ignorance would drive them to deceive themselves about what they witnessed, and they would say: "It is a gathered cloud," piled up, one part upon another, raining upon us, and not a fragment falling as punishment.

"So leave them": an imperative of truce, abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. The majority read "until they meet their day"; Abu Haywa read "hatta yalqawu," the imperfect of laqiya. "Their day": i.e., the day of their death one by one. The "sa'q" (stunning) is punishment; or the day of Badr, since they were punished on it; or the Day of Resurrection, these are views, and the third is the view of the majority, since His stunning encompasses all creatures. The majority read "yusa'qun" with a fatha on the ya'. 'Asim, Ibn Amir, Zayd ibn Ali and the people of Mecca read it [in the saying of Shibl ibn Ubada], and the people of Mecca opened it, as the majority did in the saying of Isma'il. Al-Sulami read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the 'ayn, from the quadriliteral "asa'qa."

"And indeed for those who did wrong": i.e., for these wrongdoers, "a punishment short of that": i.e., short of the Day of Resurrection and before it, which is the day of Badr and the conquest, as Ibn Abbas and others said. Al-Barra' ibn Azib and Ibn Abbas also said: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: their calamities in this world. Mujahid said: it is hunger and drought for seven years.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verses 29–49 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿فَإنَّكَ بِأعْيُنِنا﴾ ("Indeed, you are under Our eyes"): this is an expression for protection and safekeeping. It is in the plural ("eyes") because it is attached to a pronoun of plurality. When the pronoun is singular, the noun is given in the singular, as in Allah's words: ﴿ولِتُصْنَعَ عَلى عَيْنِي﴾ ("and that you may be raised under My eye") [Ta-Ha: 39]. Abu al-Sammal recited it as *bi-a'yunna* ("bi-a'yunnā"), with a single doubled nun.

﴿وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("and glorify your Lord with His praise") [Ta-Ha: 130]. Abu al-Ahwas Awf ibn Malik said: it is the well-known *tasbih*, which is saying "Subhan Allah" at every standing. Ata said: when you rise from every gathering. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Ibn Abbas said: when you rise from your sleep. It has also been said that it is the voluntary prayer, and it has been said that it is the obligatory prayer. Al-Dahhak said: when you rise to prayer, you say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You." Zayd ibn Aslam said: when you rise from the midday rest and the glorification, and that is the time of the noon prayer. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: remember Allah with your tongue when you rise from your bed until you enter into the prayer.

﴿ومِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ﴾ ("and glorify Him during part of the night"): before the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers.

﴿وإدْبارَ النُّجُومِ﴾ ("and at the retreat of the stars"): the Subh (dawn) prayer. It is related from Amr, Ali, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan that it refers to the voluntary prayers, and that *wa-idbar al-nujum* means the two rak'ahs of Fajr. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, al-Minhal ibn Amr and Ya'qub recited *wa-adbar* with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "and the aftermaths (the last parts) of the stars."

**Surat al-Najm (The Star)** is Meccan, and it has sixty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. ﴿Your companion has neither strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2]. ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3]. ﴿It is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. ﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5]. ﴿Possessor of strength; and he stood firm﴾ [al-Najm: 6]. ﴿While he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7]. ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8]. ﴿And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9]. ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. ﴿The heart did not lie in what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11]. ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. ﴿And he had certainly seen him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13]. ﴿At the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14]. ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15]. ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. ﴿The gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19]. ﴿And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 20]. ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21]. ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [al-Najm: 22]. ﴿They are not but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow not except assumption and what the souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. ﴿Or will man have whatever he wishes?﴾ [al-Najm: 24]. ﴿For to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [al-Najm: 25]. ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not benefit at all, except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26]. ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with names of females﴾ [al-Najm: 27]. ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow not except assumption, and indeed assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28]. ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ [al-Najm: 30]. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they have done and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, other than minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He is most knowing of you, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers. So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾ [al-Najm: 33], ﴿and gave a little and then withheld﴾ [al-Najm: 34]? ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35]. ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾ [al-Najm: 36], ﴿and of Abraham who fulfilled [his trust]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]? ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38], ﴿and that man will have only what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], ﴿and that his effort will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 40], ﴿then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾ [al-Najm: 41], ﴿and that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm: 42], ﴿and that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ [al-Najm: 43], ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 44], ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female﴾ [al-Najm: 45], ﴿from a sperm-drop when it is emitted﴾ [al-Najm: 46], ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾ [al-Najm: 47], ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48], ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50], ﴿and Thamud, and spared none﴾ [al-Najm: 51], ﴿and the people of Noah before, for they were more unjust and more transgressive﴾ [al-Najm: 52], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿and covered them with what covered them﴾ [al-Najm: 54]. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute?﴾ [al-Najm: 55]. ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]. ﴿The approaching [Hour] has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]. ﴿None besides Allah can disclose it﴾ [al-Najm: 58]. ﴿Do you then wonder at this statement﴾ [al-Najm: 59], ﴿and laugh and not weep﴾ [al-Najm: 60], ﴿while you are proud [and heedless]?﴾ [al-Najm: 61]. ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [al-Najm: 62].

*Al-mirrah* means strength, from *amrartu al-habl*, when one twists the rope tightly. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of a man of sound judgment and sharp intellect that he is *dhu mirrah* ("possessor of strength"). He said:

> And I am one of firm strength, a bitter one [in the face of hardship],
> when a relative rides against my relative.

*Tadalla al-'idhq tadallayan* means that it stretched from a height down toward the bottom; it is used for nearness to the height. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi. Usama al-Hudhali said:

> It hung down over us, and it was a dove's blue-gray,
> when the moss at the end of the summer heat was dry.

*Al-qab* and *al-qayb*, and *al-qadah* and *al-qid*, mean a measure. *Al-qaws* (the bow) is well known; it is an instrument for shooting arrows, and its shapes vary. *Al-sidrah* is the lote tree (the jujube tree). *Al-dhiza* means unjust, from *dhaza-hu yadhiżu-hu*, when one oppresses him. The poet said:

> The Banu Asad were unjust in their judgment,
> when they made the head like the tail.

Its original form is *dhuzā* on the pattern *fu'lā*, like *hubla* and *unthā* and *ruyyā*. What happened to it is what happened to *bayyad* so that the *ya'* is preserved. A form *fi'lā* with a kasra on the first letter does not occur in adjectives, as Sibawayh said. Tha'lab reported *mishyatun jubkā* ("a walk of a particular kind") and *rajulun kīṣā*. Others reported *imra'atun 'izhā* and *imra'atun si'lā*, but the known forms are *'izmāh* and *si'lāh*. Al-Kisa'i said: *dāza yadīzu dīzā*, *dāza yadūzu dīwzā*, and *da'aza yad'azu di'zan*.

*Al-lamam* is what is small and slight. From it comes *al-lamam*, the touch of madness. *Alamma bi-l-makan* means he stayed in a place briefly; *alamma bi-l-ta'am* means he ate only a little of the food. Al-Mubarrad said: the root meaning of *al-lamam* is to approach something without actually engaging in it; one says *alamma bi-kadha*, meaning he came close to it without mixing with it. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs use *al-ilmam* for approaching and drawing near; one says *alamma yaf'alu kadha*, meaning he almost does it. Jarir said:

> My soul, the one whom he fends off is dear to me,
> and whose visit to me is a brief encounter.

Another said:

> The meeting of the friends at the rock is a brief encounter.

*Al-ajinnah* is the plural of *janin*, which is the child in the womb. It was named so because it is hidden. *Al-ijtinan* means concealment.

*Akda*: its origin is from *al-kudyah*. It is said of one who digs a well and then reaches a rock in which digging cannot proceed: "He has been stopped (*akda*)." Then the Arabs used it for one who gives but does not complete the giving, and for one who seeks something but does not reach its end. Al-Hutay'a said:

> He gave a little, then withheld his gift,
> and whoever spends kindness among people is praised.

Al-Kisa'i and others said: *akda al-hafir* means the digger reached a hard stone or a mountain and could not dig further. *Hafara fa-akda* means he dug and reached solid ground. It is also said: *kadiyat asabi'uhu* when his fingers grew tired from digging. *Kada al-bayt* means its income decreased. Abu Zayd said: *akda al-rajul* means his goodness decreased.

*Aqna*: al-Jawhari said: *qaniya yaqna qinan*, like *ghaniya yaghna ghinan*. It is transitive by changing the vowel, so one says *qaniytu al-mal*, meaning I acquired wealth, like *shatartu 'ayn al-rajul* and *shatara-hā Allah*. After that it became transitive by a hamza or by doubling, so one says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *qannāhu Allah mālan*. The poet said:

> How many a rich man has had his wealth struck by fate,
> and how many a poor man has acquired property after destitution.

That is, *taqanna al-mal*. One also says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *arḍāhu* ("He gave him property and contentment") from *al-qinyah*. Abu Zayd said: the Arabs say of one who is given a hundred goats: "He has been given *al-qina*"; of one given a hundred sheep: "He has been given *al-ghina*"; and of one given a hundred camels: "He has been given *al-muna*."

*Al-Shi'ra* is the bright star that rises after Orion (al-Jawza'), and its rising is in the intensity of heat. It is called "the pursuer of Orion." They are the two Shi'ras: the *'Ubur* which is in Orion, and the *Ghumayṣā'* (the Dog Star) which is in the forearm. The Arabs claim that they are the sisters of Suhayl. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also called the Dog of the Mighty One (*kalb al-jabbar*). They are two Shi'ras: al-Ghumayṣa' and al-'Ubur. Among the lies of the Arabs is that Suhayl and al-Shi'ra were a married couple; Suhayl descended and became a Yemeni, so al-Shi'ra pursued him, the 'Ubur, and she crossed the Milky Way, so she was called *al-'Ubur*; and the Ghumayṣā' stayed behind because she was less visible than the other.

*Azifa*: it drew near. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

> Youth has departed, and this gray hair has drawn near,
> and I see no departed youth coming back.

Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

> The departure has drawn near, but our saddles
> are still on our mounts, as if it were already.

It is also narrated as *afida al-tarahhul*.

*Samada*: he was heedless and played. The poet said:

> Surely you, O man, are heedless,
> as if you will never perish, and you are not destroyed.

Another said:

> It was said: "Rise, look at them,
> then leave aside the sumud."

Abu Ubayda said: *al-sumud* is singing in the language of Himyar. They say: "O girl, *usmudi* for us," meaning sing for us.

(p-151) When God Almighty's oath concerning the occurrence of the punishment had preceded, and He had mentioned some matters concerning the circumstances of those who are punished and those who are saved, He commanded him to admonish, warning the disbeliever and giving good news to the believer, and calling to God by spreading His message. Then He negated from him what the disbelievers attributed to him of soothsaying (kihanah) and madness, since these two were ways of reporting some unseen matters, and the jinn had a connection with humans through them. Among those who attributed soothsaying to him was Shayba ibn Rabi'a, and among those who attributed madness to him was Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'So admonish' means: persist in reminding and advising people, and let not their saying 'a soothsayer' or 'a madman' discourage you; do not pay attention to it, for it is a false and self-contradictory statement. The soothsayer needs cleverness and keenness of perception in his soothsaying, while the madman has his intellect covered; and you, by the praise of God Most High and His bounty upon you, are neither of these two, but rather you have the truth of prophethood and the soundness of intellect." End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "'By the blessing of your Lord' is connected to what the speech indicates, and it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject of 'ma' and its predicate. The meaning is: you are not, in the state of your reminding by the blessing of your Lord, a soothsayer." Abu al-Baqa' said: "The ba' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of 'bi-kahin' or 'majnun' is the implied meaning. The sense is: you are not a soothsayer nor a madman, being connected with the blessing of your Lord." End of quote. It would be a permanent (lazimah) circumstantial clause, not a transient one, because he, upon him be prayer and peace, was always connected with the blessing of his Lord. It was also said: "By the blessing of your Lord" is an oath by it, as if it were said: "By the blessing of your Lord, you are not a soothsayer nor a madman." So the object of the oath is placed between the subject and the predicate, as you say: "Zayd is not, by God, standing."

When He negated from him soothsaying and madness, which some disbelievers attributed to him, He mentioned another type of what they were saying.

It is narrated that the Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (council house), and their opinions about him (ﷺ) multiplied, until one speaker among them, who were the Banu Abd al-Dar, said, as related by al-Dahhak: "Wait for him to meet the vicissitudes of fate, for he is a poet who will perish just as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." So they dispersed upon this statement, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The saying of whoever said this reflects a deficiency of natural disposition such that he does not perceive poetry, which is speech measured in a known pattern distinct from prose that is not on that course. Undoubtedly some of them did perceive this, since there were poets among them; but they colluded with those deficient in disposition in saying, "He is a poet," denying the signs of God after their certainty of them.

Zayd ibn Ali read "yutarabbas" with ya' in the passive form, and "rayb" as nominative. "Rayb al-manun" means the calamities of time, for it does not remain in one state. The poet said:

"Wait for her (the wife) the calamity of fate; perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die."

And al-Hindi said:

"Do you lament from fate and its calamity? And time does not reproach whoever despairs."

"Say: wait": this is an imperative of threat, from those who wait for your destruction, just as you wait for my destruction.

"Do their minds command them to this?" Their intellects, with this, i.e., with their saying "soothsayer," "poet," and "madman," which is a self-contradictory statement. The Quraysh were called the people of intellect and understanding. It was said to Amr ibn al-As: "What is the matter with your people, that they did not believe, when God Most High has described them as having intellect?" He said: "Those are intellects that God has outwitted," meaning that success (tawfiq) did not accompany them.

"Or does their intellect command them": it was said that "am" here has the meaning of the interrogative hamzah, i.e., "Does their intellect command them?" Mujahid interpreted it as "bal" (rather), and the correct view is that it can be interpreted as both "bal" and the hamzah.

"Or are they a transgressing people": i.e., those who exceed the limit in obstinacy despite the manifestation of truth. Mujahid read "bal hum" in place of "am hum." The attribution of commanding to intellects is metaphorical, since when they led to that, they were treated as commanding, as in His saying: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped?" (Hud: 87). Al-Tha'labi related from al-Khalil that he said: "Every 'am' in Surat al-Tur is interrogative and not conjunctive."

"Taqawwalahu" means he fabricated it from his own self, as He said: "And if he had invented against Us some sayings" (al-Haqqah: 44). Ibn Atiyya said: "Taqawwalahu" means: he said that it was said by another; it is an expression for a specific lie. End of quote.

"Rather, they do not believe": i.e., because of their disbelief and obstinacy. Then He challenged them with His saying: "Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful": i.e., one similar to the Qur'an in its composition and arrangement, in eloquence, soundness of meanings, reports of the stories of past nations and of unseen matters. The ruling is: if they are truthful that he fabricated it, then let them say something like it, since he is one of them; so if they are truthful, let them be like him in fabricating. Al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read "bi-hadithin mithlihi" with the construct form, meaning: with the speech of a man like the Messenger in being unlettered (ummi), who did not accompany the people of knowledge nor travelled from his land; or like him in being one of them; so it is not permissible that there be anyone like him among the Arabs in eloquence. So let them bring something like what he brought, and they will never be able to do that.

"Or were they created from nothing": i.e., from nothing living like inanimate matter, so they are not commanded nor forbidden, as inanimate things are. Al-Tabari said this. It was also said: "from nothing" means: without a cause nor for the purpose of punishment or reward, so they therefore do not listen nor accept law. This is like your saying: "I did such and such without a cause," meaning "for no cause," so "min" here is causal, while in the first view it indicates the starting point.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or were they created': or were they brought into existence and measured with the measure upon which their nature is based; 'from nothing': from no measurer. Or are they the ones who created themselves, since they do not worship the Creator? 'Rather, they do not have certainty': i.e., if they are asked, 'Who created you and created the heavens and the earth?' they say, 'God,' while they doubt what they say and are not certain. Or were they created without a Lord and without a creator? I.e., or were they brought into existence and emerged into being without a god who makes them emerge and brings them into being? 'Or are they the creators' of themselves, so that they worship God and not obey His commands and not refrain from His prohibitions? Both alternatives are false, and they acknowledge that, so that proves their falsehood." Ibn Atiyya said: "Then He placed them in a position of rebuke concerning themselves: Are they the ones who created things, so that they are arrogant because of that? Then He specified among those things the heavens and the earth, for their greatness and nobility among created things. Then He judged against them that they do not have certainty and do not look in a way that leads them to certainty."

"Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?" Al-Zamakhshari said: The treasuries of provision, so that they might bestow prophethood upon whomever they wish? Or: Do they have the treasuries of His knowledge, so that they might choose for it whomever they wish, with wisdom and benefit? "Or are they the controllers": the lords who dominate, so that they could manage the affair of lordship and build matters upon their will. Ibn Atiyya said: "Or do they have independence from God Most High in all affairs, since wealth, health, strength and other things are all from the treasuries of God Most High?" Al-Zahrawi said: "It was said that by the treasuries He means knowledge, and this is a good view if considered and expanded." Al-Rummani said: "His treasuries, Exalted is He, are His capabilities." End of quote. "Al-musaytir," Ibn Abbas said: "the one who is empowered, the dominant." The majority read "al-musaytirun" with the sad; Hisham, Qunbul, and Hafs, according to one narration from him, read it with the sin, which is the original; and whoever substituted it with a sad did so because of the letter of elevation (isti'la'), which is the ta'. Khallad from Hamza, and Khallad from him, according to one narration from him, gave it the sound of the zay (ishmam).

"Or do they have a ladder" set up to the heaven, "upon which they listen": i.e., upon it or from it, since prepositions may take the place of one another. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ascending upon it." The object of "yastami'un" is omitted; its estimate is: the news of the correctness of what they claim. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: what is revealed to the angels of knowledge of the unseen, so that they might know what will occur, such as the prior destruction of Muhammad (ﷺ) before their destruction, and his victory in the end over them, as they claim.

"Then let their listener bring a clear authority": i.e., a clear proof of the truthfulness of their listening to the one who listens to them. "Or do you ask them for a reward," for belief in God, His unity, and following His law, "so they are burdened with heavy debt": that heavy, binding burden, which prompted their aversion to following you.

"Or do they have the unseen, so that they write": i.e., the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), "so that they write": i.e., they establish that for people as law, which is worship of idols, dedicating camels (tasyib al-sawa'ib), and other such practices of theirs. It was also said: the meaning is: they know when Muhammad (ﷺ), whom they await for, will die; and "write" means: they judge. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: do they have the Preserved Tablet, so that they write what is in it and report it?"

"Or do they intend a scheme": i.e., against you and your law; this is their scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa. "But those who disbelieved": i.e., they; the apparent noun is used to draw attention to the cause, or "those who disbelieved" is general, so they are included in it. "They are the ones who will be ensnared": i.e., those upon whom the consequence of their scheme returns, and whose plotting encircles them. That is because they were killed on the day of Badr, and He named their defeat a "scheme," since it was the punishment for scheming.

"Or do they have a god other than God" to protect them and defend them against the onset of their destruction? Then He declared Himself free: "Exalted is God above what they associate": with idols and images.

"And if they see a fragment of the sky falling": the Quraysh had proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among what they proposed, their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim" (al-Isra': 92). So He informed that if they saw that directly, according to their proposal, their insolence and ignorance would drive them to deceive themselves about what they witnessed, and they would say: "It is a gathered cloud," piled up, one part upon another, raining upon us, and not a fragment falling as punishment.

"So leave them": an imperative of truce, abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. The majority read "until they meet their day"; Abu Haywa read "hatta yalqawu," the imperfect of laqiya. "Their day": i.e., the day of their death one by one. The "sa'q" (stunning) is punishment; or the day of Badr, since they were punished on it; or the Day of Resurrection, these are views, and the third is the view of the majority, since His stunning encompasses all creatures. The majority read "yusa'qun" with a fatha on the ya'. 'Asim, Ibn Amir, Zayd ibn Ali and the people of Mecca read it [in the saying of Shibl ibn Ubada], and the people of Mecca opened it, as the majority did in the saying of Isma'il. Al-Sulami read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the 'ayn, from the quadriliteral "asa'qa."

"And indeed for those who did wrong": i.e., for these wrongdoers, "a punishment short of that": i.e., short of the Day of Resurrection and before it, which is the day of Badr and the conquest, as Ibn Abbas and others said. Al-Barra' ibn Azib and Ibn Abbas also said: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: their calamities in this world. Mujahid said: it is hunger and drought for seven years.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verses 29–49 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿فَإنَّكَ بِأعْيُنِنا﴾ ("Indeed, you are under Our eyes"): this is an expression for protection and safekeeping. It is in the plural ("eyes") because it is attached to a pronoun of plurality. When the pronoun is singular, the noun is given in the singular, as in Allah's words: ﴿ولِتُصْنَعَ عَلى عَيْنِي﴾ ("and that you may be raised under My eye") [Ta-Ha: 39]. Abu al-Sammal recited it as *bi-a'yunna* ("bi-a'yunnā"), with a single doubled nun.

﴿وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("and glorify your Lord with His praise") [Ta-Ha: 130]. Abu al-Ahwas Awf ibn Malik said: it is the well-known *tasbih*, which is saying "Subhan Allah" at every standing. Ata said: when you rise from every gathering. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Ibn Abbas said: when you rise from your sleep. It has also been said that it is the voluntary prayer, and it has been said that it is the obligatory prayer. Al-Dahhak said: when you rise to prayer, you say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You." Zayd ibn Aslam said: when you rise from the midday rest and the glorification, and that is the time of the noon prayer. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: remember Allah with your tongue when you rise from your bed until you enter into the prayer.

﴿ومِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ﴾ ("and glorify Him during part of the night"): before the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers.

﴿وإدْبارَ النُّجُومِ﴾ ("and at the retreat of the stars"): the Subh (dawn) prayer. It is related from Amr, Ali, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan that it refers to the voluntary prayers, and that *wa-idbar al-nujum* means the two rak'ahs of Fajr. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, al-Minhal ibn Amr and Ya'qub recited *wa-adbar* with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "and the aftermaths (the last parts) of the stars."

**Surat al-Najm (The Star)** is Meccan, and it has sixty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. ﴿Your companion has neither strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2]. ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3]. ﴿It is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. ﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5]. ﴿Possessor of strength; and he stood firm﴾ [al-Najm: 6]. ﴿While he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7]. ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8]. ﴿And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9]. ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. ﴿The heart did not lie in what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11]. ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12]. ﴿And he had certainly seen him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13]. ﴿At the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14]. ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15]. ﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. ﴿The gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. ﴿He had certainly seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19]. ﴿And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 20]. ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21]. ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [al-Najm: 22]. ﴿They are not but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow not except assumption and what the souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. ﴿Or will man have whatever he wishes?﴾ [al-Najm: 24]. ﴿For to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [al-Najm: 25]. ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not benefit at all, except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26]. ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with names of females﴾ [al-Najm: 27]. ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow not except assumption, and indeed assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28]. ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ [al-Najm: 30]. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they have done and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, other than minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He is most knowing of you, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers. So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾ [al-Najm: 33], ﴿and gave a little and then withheld﴾ [al-Najm: 34]? ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35]. ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾ [al-Najm: 36], ﴿and of Abraham who fulfilled [his trust]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]? ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38], ﴿and that man will have only what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], ﴿and that his effort will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 40], ﴿then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾ [al-Najm: 41], ﴿and that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm: 42], ﴿and that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ [al-Najm: 43], ﴿and that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 44], ﴿and that He created the two mates, male and female﴾ [al-Najm: 45], ﴿from a sperm-drop when it is emitted﴾ [al-Najm: 46], ﴿and that upon Him is the second creation﴾ [al-Najm: 47], ﴿and that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48], ﴿and that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50], ﴿and Thamud, and spared none﴾ [al-Najm: 51], ﴿and the people of Noah before, for they were more unjust and more transgressive﴾ [al-Najm: 52], ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53], ﴿and covered them with what covered them﴾ [al-Najm: 54]. ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute?﴾ [al-Najm: 55]. ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]. ﴿The approaching [Hour] has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]. ﴿None besides Allah can disclose it﴾ [al-Najm: 58]. ﴿Do you then wonder at this statement﴾ [al-Najm: 59], ﴿and laugh and not weep﴾ [al-Najm: 60], ﴿while you are proud [and heedless]?﴾ [al-Najm: 61]. ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [al-Najm: 62].

*Al-mirrah* means strength, from *amrartu al-habl*, when one twists the rope tightly. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of a man of sound judgment and sharp intellect that he is *dhu mirrah* ("possessor of strength"). He said:

> And I am one of firm strength, a bitter one [in the face of hardship],
> when a relative rides against my relative.

*Tadalla al-'idhq tadallayan* means that it stretched from a height down toward the bottom; it is used for nearness to the height. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi. Usama al-Hudhali said:

> It hung down over us, and it was a dove's blue-gray,
> when the moss at the end of the summer heat was dry.

*Al-qab* and *al-qayb*, and *al-qadah* and *al-qid*, mean a measure. *Al-qaws* (the bow) is well known; it is an instrument for shooting arrows, and its shapes vary. *Al-sidrah* is the lote tree (the jujube tree). *Al-dhiza* means unjust, from *dhaza-hu yadhiżu-hu*, when one oppresses him. The poet said:

> The Banu Asad were unjust in their judgment,
> when they made the head like the tail.

Its original form is *dhuzā* on the pattern *fu'lā*, like *hubla* and *unthā* and *ruyyā*. What happened to it is what happened to *bayyad* so that the *ya'* is preserved. A form *fi'lā* with a kasra on the first letter does not occur in adjectives, as Sibawayh said. Tha'lab reported *mishyatun jubkā* ("a walk of a particular kind") and *rajulun kīṣā*. Others reported *imra'atun 'izhā* and *imra'atun si'lā*, but the known forms are *'izmāh* and *si'lāh*. Al-Kisa'i said: *dāza yadīzu dīzā*, *dāza yadūzu dīwzā*, and *da'aza yad'azu di'zan*.

*Al-lamam* is what is small and slight. From it comes *al-lamam*, the touch of madness. *Alamma bi-l-makan* means he stayed in a place briefly; *alamma bi-l-ta'am* means he ate only a little of the food. Al-Mubarrad said: the root meaning of *al-lamam* is to approach something without actually engaging in it; one says *alamma bi-kadha*, meaning he came close to it without mixing with it. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs use *al-ilmam* for approaching and drawing near; one says *alamma yaf'alu kadha*, meaning he almost does it. Jarir said:

> My soul, the one whom he fends off is dear to me,
> and whose visit to me is a brief encounter.

Another said:

> The meeting of the friends at the rock is a brief encounter.

*Al-ajinnah* is the plural of *janin*, which is the child in the womb. It was named so because it is hidden. *Al-ijtinan* means concealment.

*Akda*: its origin is from *al-kudyah*. It is said of one who digs a well and then reaches a rock in which digging cannot proceed: "He has been stopped (*akda*)." Then the Arabs used it for one who gives but does not complete the giving, and for one who seeks something but does not reach its end. Al-Hutay'a said:

> He gave a little, then withheld his gift,
> and whoever spends kindness among people is praised.

Al-Kisa'i and others said: *akda al-hafir* means the digger reached a hard stone or a mountain and could not dig further. *Hafara fa-akda* means he dug and reached solid ground. It is also said: *kadiyat asabi'uhu* when his fingers grew tired from digging. *Kada al-bayt* means its income decreased. Abu Zayd said: *akda al-rajul* means his goodness decreased.

*Aqna*: al-Jawhari said: *qaniya yaqna qinan*, like *ghaniya yaghna ghinan*. It is transitive by changing the vowel, so one says *qaniytu al-mal*, meaning I acquired wealth, like *shatartu 'ayn al-rajul* and *shatara-hā Allah*. After that it became transitive by a hamza or by doubling, so one says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *qannāhu Allah mālan*. The poet said:

> How many a rich man has had his wealth struck by fate,
> and how many a poor man has acquired property after destitution.

That is, *taqanna al-mal*. One also says *aqnāhu Allah mālan* and *arḍāhu* ("He gave him property and contentment") from *al-qinyah*. Abu Zayd said: the Arabs say of one who is given a hundred goats: "He has been given *al-qina*"; of one given a hundred sheep: "He has been given *al-ghina*"; and of one given a hundred camels: "He has been given *al-muna*."

*Al-Shi'ra* is the bright star that rises after Orion (al-Jawza'), and its rising is in the intensity of heat. It is called "the pursuer of Orion." They are the two Shi'ras: the *'Ubur* which is in Orion, and the *Ghumayṣā'* (the Dog Star) which is in the forearm. The Arabs claim that they are the sisters of Suhayl. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also called the Dog of the Mighty One (*kalb al-jabbar*). They are two Shi'ras: al-Ghumayṣa' and al-'Ubur. Among the lies of the Arabs is that Suhayl and al-Shi'ra were a married couple; Suhayl descended and became a Yemeni, so al-Shi'ra pursued him, the 'Ubur, and she crossed the Milky Way, so she was called *al-'Ubur*; and the Ghumayṣā' stayed behind because she was less visible than the other.

*Azifa*: it drew near. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

> Youth has departed, and this gray hair has drawn near,
> and I see no departed youth coming back.

Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

> The departure has drawn near, but our saddles
> are still on our mounts, as if it were already.

It is also narrated as *afida al-tarahhul*.

*Samada*: he was heedless and played. The poet said:

> Surely you, O man, are heedless,
> as if you will never perish, and you are not destroyed.

Another said:

> It was said: "Rise, look at them,
> then leave aside the sumud."

Abu Ubayda said: *al-sumud* is singing in the language of Himyar. They say: "O girl, *usmudi* for us," meaning sing for us.

(p-151) When God Almighty's oath concerning the occurrence of the punishment had preceded, and He had mentioned some matters concerning the circumstances of those who are punished and those who are saved, He commanded him to admonish, warning the disbeliever and giving good news to the believer, and calling to God by spreading His message. Then He negated from him what the disbelievers attributed to him of soothsaying (kihanah) and madness, since these two were ways of reporting some unseen matters, and the jinn had a connection with humans through them. Among those who attributed soothsaying to him was Shayba ibn Rabi'a, and among those who attributed madness to him was Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'So admonish' means: persist in reminding and advising people, and let not their saying 'a soothsayer' or 'a madman' discourage you; do not pay attention to it, for it is a false and self-contradictory statement. The soothsayer needs cleverness and keenness of perception in his soothsaying, while the madman has his intellect covered; and you, by the praise of God Most High and His bounty upon you, are neither of these two, but rather you have the truth of prophethood and the soundness of intellect." End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "'By the blessing of your Lord' is connected to what the speech indicates, and it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject of 'ma' and its predicate. The meaning is: you are not, in the state of your reminding by the blessing of your Lord, a soothsayer." Abu al-Baqa' said: "The ba' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of 'bi-kahin' or 'majnun' is the implied meaning. The sense is: you are not a soothsayer nor a madman, being connected with the blessing of your Lord." End of quote. It would be a permanent (lazimah) circumstantial clause, not a transient one, because he, upon him be prayer and peace, was always connected with the blessing of his Lord. It was also said: "By the blessing of your Lord" is an oath by it, as if it were said: "By the blessing of your Lord, you are not a soothsayer nor a madman." So the object of the oath is placed between the subject and the predicate, as you say: "Zayd is not, by God, standing."

When He negated from him soothsaying and madness, which some disbelievers attributed to him, He mentioned another type of what they were saying.

It is narrated that the Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (council house), and their opinions about him (ﷺ) multiplied, until one speaker among them, who were the Banu Abd al-Dar, said, as related by al-Dahhak: "Wait for him to meet the vicissitudes of fate, for he is a poet who will perish just as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." So they dispersed upon this statement, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The saying of whoever said this reflects a deficiency of natural disposition such that he does not perceive poetry, which is speech measured in a known pattern distinct from prose that is not on that course. Undoubtedly some of them did perceive this, since there were poets among them; but they colluded with those deficient in disposition in saying, "He is a poet," denying the signs of God after their certainty of them.

Zayd ibn Ali read "yutarabbas" with ya' in the passive form, and "rayb" as nominative. "Rayb al-manun" means the calamities of time, for it does not remain in one state. The poet said:

"Wait for her (the wife) the calamity of fate; perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die."

And al-Hindi said:

"Do you lament from fate and its calamity? And time does not reproach whoever despairs."

"Say: wait": this is an imperative of threat, from those who wait for your destruction, just as you wait for my destruction.

"Do their minds command them to this?" Their intellects, with this, i.e., with their saying "soothsayer," "poet," and "madman," which is a self-contradictory statement. The Quraysh were called the people of intellect and understanding. It was said to Amr ibn al-As: "What is the matter with your people, that they did not believe, when God Most High has described them as having intellect?" He said: "Those are intellects that God has outwitted," meaning that success (tawfiq) did not accompany them.

"Or does their intellect command them": it was said that "am" here has the meaning of the interrogative hamzah, i.e., "Does their intellect command them?" Mujahid interpreted it as "bal" (rather), and the correct view is that it can be interpreted as both "bal" and the hamzah.

"Or are they a transgressing people": i.e., those who exceed the limit in obstinacy despite the manifestation of truth. Mujahid read "bal hum" in place of "am hum." The attribution of commanding to intellects is metaphorical, since when they led to that, they were treated as commanding, as in His saying: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped?" (Hud: 87). Al-Tha'labi related from al-Khalil that he said: "Every 'am' in Surat al-Tur is interrogative and not conjunctive."

"Taqawwalahu" means he fabricated it from his own self, as He said: "And if he had invented against Us some sayings" (al-Haqqah: 44). Ibn Atiyya said: "Taqawwalahu" means: he said that it was said by another; it is an expression for a specific lie. End of quote.

"Rather, they do not believe": i.e., because of their disbelief and obstinacy. Then He challenged them with His saying: "Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful": i.e., one similar to the Qur'an in its composition and arrangement, in eloquence, soundness of meanings, reports of the stories of past nations and of unseen matters. The ruling is: if they are truthful that he fabricated it, then let them say something like it, since he is one of them; so if they are truthful, let them be like him in fabricating. Al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read "bi-hadithin mithlihi" with the construct form, meaning: with the speech of a man like the Messenger in being unlettered (ummi), who did not accompany the people of knowledge nor travelled from his land; or like him in being one of them; so it is not permissible that there be anyone like him among the Arabs in eloquence. So let them bring something like what he brought, and they will never be able to do that.

"Or were they created from nothing": i.e., from nothing living like inanimate matter, so they are not commanded nor forbidden, as inanimate things are. Al-Tabari said this. It was also said: "from nothing" means: without a cause nor for the purpose of punishment or reward, so they therefore do not listen nor accept law. This is like your saying: "I did such and such without a cause," meaning "for no cause," so "min" here is causal, while in the first view it indicates the starting point.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or were they created': or were they brought into existence and measured with the measure upon which their nature is based; 'from nothing': from no measurer. Or are they the ones who created themselves, since they do not worship the Creator? 'Rather, they do not have certainty': i.e., if they are asked, 'Who created you and created the heavens and the earth?' they say, 'God,' while they doubt what they say and are not certain. Or were they created without a Lord and without a creator? I.e., or were they brought into existence and emerged into being without a god who makes them emerge and brings them into being? 'Or are they the creators' of themselves, so that they worship God and not obey His commands and not refrain from His prohibitions? Both alternatives are false, and they acknowledge that, so that proves their falsehood." Ibn Atiyya said: "Then He placed them in a position of rebuke concerning themselves: Are they the ones who created things, so that they are arrogant because of that? Then He specified among those things the heavens and the earth, for their greatness and nobility among created things. Then He judged against them that they do not have certainty and do not look in a way that leads them to certainty."

"Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?" Al-Zamakhshari said: The treasuries of provision, so that they might bestow prophethood upon whomever they wish? Or: Do they have the treasuries of His knowledge, so that they might choose for it whomever they wish, with wisdom and benefit? "Or are they the controllers": the lords who dominate, so that they could manage the affair of lordship and build matters upon their will. Ibn Atiyya said: "Or do they have independence from God Most High in all affairs, since wealth, health, strength and other things are all from the treasuries of God Most High?" Al-Zahrawi said: "It was said that by the treasuries He means knowledge, and this is a good view if considered and expanded." Al-Rummani said: "His treasuries, Exalted is He, are His capabilities." End of quote. "Al-musaytir," Ibn Abbas said: "the one who is empowered, the dominant." The majority read "al-musaytirun" with the sad; Hisham, Qunbul, and Hafs, according to one narration from him, read it with the sin, which is the original; and whoever substituted it with a sad did so because of the letter of elevation (isti'la'), which is the ta'. Khallad from Hamza, and Khallad from him, according to one narration from him, gave it the sound of the zay (ishmam).

"Or do they have a ladder" set up to the heaven, "upon which they listen": i.e., upon it or from it, since prepositions may take the place of one another. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ascending upon it." The object of "yastami'un" is omitted; its estimate is: the news of the correctness of what they claim. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: what is revealed to the angels of knowledge of the unseen, so that they might know what will occur, such as the prior destruction of Muhammad (ﷺ) before their destruction, and his victory in the end over them, as they claim.

"Then let their listener bring a clear authority": i.e., a clear proof of the truthfulness of their listening to the one who listens to them. "Or do you ask them for a reward," for belief in God, His unity, and following His law, "so they are burdened with heavy debt": that heavy, binding burden, which prompted their aversion to following you.

"Or do they have the unseen, so that they write": i.e., the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), "so that they write": i.e., they establish that for people as law, which is worship of idols, dedicating camels (tasyib al-sawa'ib), and other such practices of theirs. It was also said: the meaning is: they know when Muhammad (ﷺ), whom they await for, will die; and "write" means: they judge. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: do they have the Preserved Tablet, so that they write what is in it and report it?"

"Or do they intend a scheme": i.e., against you and your law; this is their scheme against him in the Dar al-Nadwa. "But those who disbelieved": i.e., they; the apparent noun is used to draw attention to the cause, or "those who disbelieved" is general, so they are included in it. "They are the ones who will be ensnared": i.e., those upon whom the consequence of their scheme returns, and whose plotting encircles them. That is because they were killed on the day of Badr, and He named their defeat a "scheme," since it was the punishment for scheming.

"Or do they have a god other than God" to protect them and defend them against the onset of their destruction? Then He declared Himself free: "Exalted is God above what they associate": with idols and images.

"And if they see a fragment of the sky falling": the Quraysh had proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among what they proposed, their saying: "Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim" (al-Isra': 92). So He informed that if they saw that directly, according to their proposal, their insolence and ignorance would drive them to deceive themselves about what they witnessed, and they would say: "It is a gathered cloud," piled up, one part upon another, raining upon us, and not a fragment falling as punishment.

"So leave them": an imperative of truce, abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. The majority read "until they meet their day"; Abu Haywa read "hatta yalqawu," the imperfect of laqiya. "Their day": i.e., the day of their death one by one. The "sa'q" (stunning) is punishment; or the day of Badr, since they were punished on it; or the Day of Resurrection, these are views, and the third is the view of the majority, since His stunning encompasses all creatures. The majority read "yusa'qun" with a fatha on the ya'. 'Asim, Ibn Amir, Zayd ibn Ali and the people of Mecca read it [in the saying of Shibl ibn Ubada], and the people of Mecca opened it, as the majority did in the saying of Isma'il. Al-Sulami read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the 'ayn, from the quadriliteral "asa'qa."

"And indeed for those who did wrong": i.e., for these wrongdoers, "a punishment short of that": i.e., short of the Day of Resurrection and before it, which is the day of Badr and the conquest, as Ibn Abbas and others said. Al-Barra' ibn Azib and Ibn Abbas also said: it is the punishment of the grave. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: their calamities in this world. Mujahid said: it is hunger and drought for seven years.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 52, verses 29–49 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿فَإنَّكَ بِأعْيُنِنا﴾ ("Indeed, you are under Our eyes"): this is an expression for protection and safekeeping. It is in the plural ("eyes") because it is attached to a pronoun of plurality. When the pronoun is singular, the noun is given in the singular, as in Allah's words: ﴿ولِتُصْنَعَ عَلى عَيْنِي﴾ ("and that you may be raised under My eye") [Ta-Ha: 39]. Abu al-Sammal recited it as *bi-a'yunna* ("bi-a'yunnā"), with a single doubled nun.

﴿وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("and glorify your Lord with His praise") [Ta-Ha: 130]. Abu al-Ahwas Awf ibn Malik said: it is the well-known *tasbih*, which is saying "Subhan Allah" at every standing. Ata said: when you rise from every gathering. This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Ibn Abbas said: when you rise from your sleep. It has also been said that it is the voluntary prayer, and it has been said that it is the obligatory prayer. Al-Dahhak said: when you rise to prayer, you say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You." Zayd ibn Aslam said: when you rise from the midday rest and the glorification, and that is the time of the noon prayer. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: remember Allah with your tongue when you rise from your bed until you enter into the prayer.

﴿ومِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ﴾ ("and glorify Him during part of the night"): before the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers.

﴿وإدْبارَ النُّجُومِ﴾ ("and at the retreat of the stars"): the Subh (dawn) prayer. It is related from Amr, Ali, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan that it refers to the voluntary prayers, and that *wa-idbar al-nujum* means the two rak'ahs of Fajr. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, al-Minhal ibn Amr and Ya'qub recited *wa-adbar* with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "and the aftermaths (the last parts) of the stars."
